KizamuBeam takes you from the first idea to the finished piece in one app: draw and write directly on the workspace, turn photos into engravings, generate boxes, gears and slot-together models, check everything in 3D and send the job straight to your laser. It is free software (GPL-3.0), needs no account and runs on macOS, Windows and Linux.

This manual is new and grows with every release. Pages that are not written yet point to the complete feature list, which describes every function with its menu path. The manual lives in the same repository as the app. Found a mistake, or want to add a page or a translation? See Contributing to the manual. Questions are welcome on Discord.
The manual is written in Markdown and lives in the KizamuBeam repository, in the manual/ folder. Every change goes through a pull request and is published automatically once it is merged.
Every page has an Edit this page link at the bottom. It opens the file on GitHub, where you can change it and propose the change as a pull request, right in the browser.

Path Content manual/docs/ English pages (the original) manual/i18n/de/docusaurus-plugin-content-docs/current/ German pages manual/i18n/it/docusaurus-plugin-content-docs/current/ Italian pages manual/i18n/<lang>/*.json Translated navigation, footer and sidebar labels manual/static/img/ Screenshots and images Each folder in docs/ is a chapter in the sidebar. Its _category_.json sets the chapter’s title and position; sidebar_position in a page’s front matter sets the order inside the chapter. A folder that only holds an index.md appears as a single page; once it gets more pages, add a _category_.json and translate its label in manual/i18n/<lang>/docusaurus-plugin-content-docs/current.json.

A page starts with front matter: --- sidebar_position: 2 title: Nesting description: One sentence that search engines and link previews show. --- # Nesting Text … Guidelines: Write for users, not developers: say what something is for, then where to find it (Menu → Entry) and how to use it. Use the names the app shows in English, in bold. Short sentences, one topic per page, link to related pages. Do not compare KizamuBeam with other laser programs. New features: when a pull request adds a user-visible function, it should also add or update the matching manual page (at least in English).

Save screenshots as PNG or WebP in manual/static/img/, with the language in the name, e.g. nesting-dialog-en.png and nesting-dialog-de.png. Use the light theme and a window of about 1500 × 950 pixels, so that screenshots look alike. Take them with the current version of the app, and replace them when the interface changes. Embed them with a description for screen readers: ![Nesting dialog with spacing and rotation settings](/img/nesting-dialog-en.png).

Diagrams are written as Mermaid code blocks and drawn on the page: ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Draw] --> B[Preview] --> C[Start] ``` Videos are embedded with an iframe, for example from YouTube without cookies: <iframe width="560" height="315" src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/VIDEO_ID" title="Video title" allowFullScreen></iframe> Info boxes use :::tip, :::note, :::info and :::warning.

English is the original. German and Italian pages have the same file names and folders under manual/i18n/<lang>/docusaurus-plugin-content-docs/current/. If a translation is missing, the English page is shown instead, so a page can be translated later. To add a new language, add it to i18n.locales in manual/docusaurus.config.ts and run npm run write-translations -- --locale <lang> in manual/ to create the label files.

You need Node.js 20 or newer. cd manual npm ci npm start # English, reloads on every change npm run start:de # German npm run build # everything, as it will be published npm run serve # look at the result of the build The search only works in the result of npm run build.
Extension packs (.kzp files) add device presets, templates, material library entries and library items (motifs, images, design elements) to KizamuBeam, without a new version of the app.

Open File → Extensions …. Either pick a pack from the official catalogue and install it with one click, or click Install … and choose a .kzp file. You can also drag a .kzp file onto the workspace. The dialog lists what the pack contains and whether it is an update. Confirm to install. After installing: templates appear under File → New from template … → From extensions, device presets appear in the device list under their manufacturer (or under “From extensions”), marked with the pack name, materials are copied into the material library, motifs and design elements appear in the library. Removing a pack in the same window removes its entries again.

A pack contains data only, never program code. KizamuBeam checks every entry before installing, and device presets from packs cannot bring start or end scripts or any other commands for your machine. The official catalogue is signed, and every pack in it is verified against its checksum.

The official catalogue is published together with this manual and the website, and File → Extensions … always shows its current state. It contains these packs: Pack Contents Needs Example pack (org.kizamubeam.example) One of each kind of content: a device preset (GRBL laser 300 × 200), two material entries (cut and engrave for poplar plywood), a template (round coaster with a line of text) and three library items (heart, double frame, star). The values are examples, not measured settings. KizamuBeam 1.2.1 or newer The example pack is meant as a starting point for your own packs. Packs from other makers are listed here once they have been checked and added to the catalogue. Until then, install third-party packs only from sources you trust: KizamuBeam checks their content, but cannot tell whether settings suit your machine.
A pack is a single JSON file. The format is described in the developer documentation: Extension packs. Packs for the official catalogue are submitted as a pull request to the packs/ folder.

Page What it covers Customizing and settings Windows, toolbars, language, theme, transferring and syncing settings AI agents (MCP) Letting an AI assistant work on your design The parametric parts such as gears, boxes and 3D models have their own chapter: Generators.

KizamuBeam can be controlled by an AI assistant through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The assistant can read your project, draw, run generators, check the design and, if you allow it, ask the laser to start. Every machine action still needs your confirmation in KizamuBeam.

Open File → AI Agents (MCP) …. Access is off by default. Switch the server on. It runs only on your own computer, at http://127.0.0.1:47800/mcp, and is not reachable from the network. Choose the access level (see below). Copy the token and the configuration into your AI client. For clients that only speak stdio, start the bridge with kizamubeam --mcp-stdio.

Level The assistant may Read only read the document, layers, materials, devices and fonts, get a preview image and a time estimate Read and design additionally create and change objects: shapes, text, QR codes and barcodes, Boolean operations, offset, path tools, arrays, nesting, joints, living hinges, pattern fill, generators, 3D models, parameters, templates, the library, series, layers, pages and files Also generate G-code additionally create G-code, without sending it to the machine Also operate the laser additionally connect, pause, stop and request a job, a frame or homing The laser level lasts only until KizamuBeam is closed.

An assistant never sends raw G-code to the laser. It can only request a job, a frame or homing, which starts only after you confirm it in KizamuBeam. Jobs must stay inside the work area and the device limits. Pause and stop always work. Every machine action is logged.
Each call of the assistant is one step in the undo history, named after the tool it used. Use Ctrl+Z or the History window to go back.

"Make a finger-jointed box with an inside size of 120 × 80 × 60 mm from 3 mm plywood." "Check the design and fix what you can." "Put the names from this list on name tags, one page each." "Turn this STL file into a rib model."

With several objects selected, the alignment button group in the main toolbar (and Arrange → Align and distribute) aligns edges or centres and distributes objects evenly. Keyboard: L R T B for left, right, top, bottom, C and E for the centres.

Tools → Array makes many copies at once, with a live preview. Bézier curves are copied exactly. Grid Array … (Ctrl+Shift+A): columns and rows, with the gap between copies or the distance between their centres, direction, an offset for every other row or column (for a brick layout) and optional mirroring of every other row or column. Circular Array …: copies in a circle around a centre point.

Arrange → Nest … (also in the Toolbox) arranges the selected parts by their real outlines, not just their bounding boxes, to save material. Where: the work area, a material size (width × height at a position), or a selected shape as the sheet, for example the outline of a scrap piece. Settings: Spacing between parts and to the edge (allow for the kerf). Rotation: none, 180° only, or in 90°, 45°, 15° or 5° steps. The corner to start from. Precision: fast, normal or thorough. Normal and thorough try several orders and keep the best. Small parts can go into holes of larger ones, and other objects on the page are avoided. What doesn’t fit goes onto new pages. Things that belong together move together: holes drawn as separate shapes, engravings and text on a part, generator assemblies. Nesting is one undo step.

Toolbox → Copy and Arrange → Pattern fill fills a closed shape with a seamless pattern made of real vectors, for decorating surfaces. Select the target shape. Pick a tile: one of 13 built-in patterns (honeycomb, scales, waves, Truchet, rings, diamonds, herringbone, basket weave, stars, dots, circle grid, chevron, ogee), a pattern you saved, or your own objects (a rectangle around them sets the tile frame). Choose how tiles repeat: grid, brick, half drop, mirrored, rotated by 90° (pinwheel) or hexagonal, with offset, spacing (negative = overlap), size, rotation and shift. At the edge the pattern is clipped exactly, or only whole tiles are kept; a margin keeps the outline free, and text, images and codes on the shape are kept free automatically. Lines where tiles meet are cleaned up, so nothing is lasered twice. Wrap edges lets lines that leave the tile continue in the neighbouring one. The result can be lines (to engrave, score or cut) or areas for fill layers. The pattern stays one object: double-click it to change any setting. Save as pattern stores tile and settings in the library.
With a camera above the bed, you see the material right under your design and can place the design exactly where it belongs.

Open the Camera window and choose a camera: a USB camera, or a network camera that delivers an MJPEG stream or single images over http://, for example an ESP32-CAM or the virtual camera of the Virtual Machine. The image is undistorted and placed under the objects on the workspace. You can set its opacity and update it once or continuously. Insert as Image puts the current picture on the T1 layer, for example to trace it. On macOS the system asks for camera permission on the first connection. A device can have several cameras, each with its own calibration, all shown at the same time.

The camera has to learn where the bed is in its picture: Start the calibration in the Camera window. Let the laser mark a grid of markers (2 × 2 up to 5 × 5) on a piece of scrap, or save the markers as G-code. Take a picture and click each marker in the photo. KizamuBeam computes the placement and, from 3 × 3 markers, the lens distortion. It shows the remaining error in mm and an undistorted check view. The calibration dialog has its own controls to connect, home and jog the machine. Calibrations can be exported as a .kzb-camera file and imported on another computer with the same camera and mounting.

The Camera window can shift, stretch and rotate the overlay slightly without a new calibration, and adjust brightness, contrast, saturation and gamma or show the image in grey. These settings only change the display, not the calibration.

A camera on the laser head sees only a small area. KizamuBeam calibrates it with small markers around the head position and places each picture at the head position where it was taken. Capture bed or Capture selection moves the head over the area (laser off) and stitches the pictures together. The field of view is shown dashed at the head position.

Place on workpieces (in the Camera window, or Toolbox → Copy and Arrange) finds identical workpieces in the camera image and puts the selected design on each of them, in the right position and rotation. Lay the workpieces on the bed and take a picture. Select your design. Either draw the workpiece outline around it (the outline can lie anywhere, for example next to the bed), or put the design on one of the detected workpieces. In the dialog, click workpieces to include or exclude them, turn them by 90° or 180°, and check the dashed orange preview on the workspace. Workpieces are separated from the bed by brightness, or more reliably with a remembered photo of the empty bed. Sensitivity and minimum size are adjustable. Options: also place the outline, hide the template afterwards, group per workpiece. One undo step. For batches with a fixed layout, a jig is often more precise.

KizamuBeam can turn ordinary shapes into parts that slot or glue together. The generators build complete boxes, drawers and shelves; the tools on this page work on shapes you drew or imported yourself.

The Joint tool (the Joint button in the tools toolbar, or Toolbox → Joints and Bending → Joints) adds a joint between two straight edges: Choose the tool. The status bar asks for the first edge. Click the first straight edge. It gets the fingers or tenons. Click the second straight edge. It gets the counterpart or the slots. If the second "edge" is a single drawn line, the line is replaced by slots, which is how you put a mortise in the middle of a panel. Set the options in the dialog and confirm. The result stays an ordinary, editable path. The joint remembers the material thickness, so Resize slots can update it later. Type Use Finger joint Box corners: interlocking fingers along both edges. Mortise and tenon Tenons on one panel, matching slots (mortises) in the other, also in the middle of a panel. Cross lap Both parts get slots of material thickness and are slid into each other; the depth is split between the two (for example 50 % each). Several slots make grid inserts and bottle dividers. Snap-fit joint Tabs with two flexible tongues and catch hooks; overhang, hook length and spring slot are adjustable. Holds without glue. Hook joint L-shaped hook tabs: insert, then slide. The slot is lengthened by the hook length. Wedged tenon Tenons pass through the other panel and have a wedge hole; the wedges are created too. T-slot A screw slot with a nut window between every two tenons, and a matching screw hole in the other panel. Lid hinge (with pin) See Lid hinge below. Common settings are the material thickness, the kerf (fingers and tenons are drawn wider, gaps and slots narrower, so the parts have their nominal size after cutting) and the clearance per side (negative values give a press fit). Once the material is calibrated, the tool proposes kerf and clearance for the chosen type.

A lid hinge with a pin lets a box lid open beyond 90°. Start it from the Toolbox → Boxes and Furniture → Lid hinge, or choose Lid hinge (with pin) in the Joint tool: Click the top edge of the back wall. Click the back edge of the lid. Both panels get slots, and knuckles with pin holes are created next to them. The outer knuckles belong to the box, the ones in between to the lid. Glue the knuckles into the slots and push a pin (wire, dowel, nail or filament) through all eyes. Number of knuckles, pin diameter, pin clearance and the wall around the hole are adjustable.

Toolbox → Joints and Bending → Living Hinge fills a selected closed shape with a cut pattern, so the board bends in that area. Patterns: straight cuts, waves, diamonds, honeycomb, triangles, weave and spiral. The dialog shows a live preview and starts with values that suit the material thickness. The cuts are exact lines and Bézier curves. Put the hinge area on the cut layer of the part. Plywood and MDF bend best across the grain of the top veneer; test on an offcut first.

Material is rarely exactly as thick as it says. Toolbox → Joints and Bending → Resize slots finds the slots that another plate slots into, also in imported SVG or DXF designs and in parts that are already plain paths: cut-outs (mortises, including a separate rectangle inside a plate), notches cut in from the edge (cross slots, half laps), each with two parallel sides and deeper than wide. Finger joint gaps are left alone. The dialog suggests the most common slot width (or the thickness of the layer's material), marks the slots it found in orange, and makes every slot wider or narrower by the difference to the new thickness, so the play stays the same. It searches the selection, or the whole page when nothing is selected. Boxes, drawers, inserts and shelves from the generators get the new thickness as a parameter instead. One undo step.

Tools → Place slots / notches … puts rectangular slots or notches into a closed shape at an exact distance: Select one closed vector object. In the tool's preview, pick a reference corner (red) and a straight edge (orange). Enter the distance along the edge and choose whether it is measured to the first outer edge, the centre or the second outer edge of the slot. You can stage several cuts across different edges before you apply them. Apply is one undo step, Cancel discards everything, and a double-click on the part reopens the tool.

Window → 3D View (or the 3D button in the main toolbar) shows your parts assembled, as they will be after cutting: Boxes, drawers, inserts, shelves and gear pairs from the generators are put together automatically. The gears of a gear pair can turn. Parts joined with the Joint tool are assembled at the joined edges: one part lies flat, the others stand on it. Other closed shapes on cut layers lie flat with an adjustable thickness; nested shapes become holes. Layered, rib and disc models from 3D models are shown assembled. Turn the view with the mouse, or use the preset views (3D, top, front). The Explode slider pulls the parts apart. With nothing selected, the view shows the whole page; a selected part always brings its whole assembly. Collisions: where two parts intersect (for example with a press fit or a slot that is too narrow), the area turns red, and the status line names the parts and the volume. Engravings: with the checkbox Engravings, fills, engraved lines, text and processed images appear on the face that was up during lasering, with a slight depth. Engravings that lie on no part are not drawn, and when lasering they would hit the work surface. The status line counts them (“1 engraving without part”); a click on the count selects them on the workspace.

Each cut layer can get its own look in the layer dialog under Appearance in 3D: 21 presets such as poplar and birch plywood, beech, oak, walnut, bamboo, MDF, cardboard, cork, leather, slate, granite, clear, coloured and opaque acrylic, glass, anodized aluminium and stainless steel, each with an optional custom colour. Engravings look different per material: dark burn on wood, light grey on slate, frosted white on acrylic and glass. Layers without their own look take it from the name of their material library entry. To show a flat piece without a cut (a slate coaster, for example), draw its outline on a layer with output off: it becomes the plate. The same works for raw stock: draw a rectangle of the sheet size on such a layer, and the engravings and the cut parts lying on it show up on the sheet. Parts that lie inside the sheet stay parts, and the sheet gets holes in their place. The checkbox “Stock” in the 3D window hides the sheets when you only want to look at the parts.

Tick Mockup in the 3D window to hide the grid and the red collision marks and get soft shadows and a background of your choice (studio gradient, white, grey, dark or like the interface). Save image … stores the current view as a PNG at double resolution.

Laser → Check Design (or Window → Design Check) looks for problems on the current page and marks every finding on the workspace. Click a finding to select the objects and zoom to the spot; where possible, a button fixes it in one undo step. It finds, among other things: lines that would be cut twice, outlines that are almost closed (gap up to 1 mm), and single lines that form an outline but are not joined, open lines on fill layers, which would be skipped, bridges between two cuts narrower than the minimum bridge (default 1 mm, kerf taken into account), cut-outs too small for the kerf, objects outside the work area, engravings that lie on no cut part (they are missing in the 3D view and would hit the work surface; nothing is reported if the page has no cut part at all, because then everything lies on a finished object), elements that an SVG or DXF import had to skip, the fit of slot-together joints from the generators and the Joint tool against material thickness and kerf (too tight, very tight, very loose). The assembly check goes further for generator assemblies (box, drawer, insert, shelf, disc sphere, layered and rib model): every piece must be one connected part, and the check puts the parts together one by one. If no order works with straight moves, you get a warning. The settings (minimum bridge, kerf width, gap size, layers that only engrave) are in the same window, together with the option to check before every job. If problems remain when a job starts, KizamuBeam lists them and asks whether to go on.

Edit → Settings … holds all application-wide preferences in one window, with a sidebar (General, Appearance, Workspace and snapping, Mouse and keyboard, Machines and services, Extensions and fonts) and a search across all of them. Changes take effect with OK; Cancel discards them, and Defaults resets the current section. Settings that also have a menu entry (language, theme, snapping, grid and so on) are the same values: changing one place changes the other.
View → Language: English, German or Italian. The default follows the system language. View → Theme (or the button at the far right of the main toolbar): light or dark. The default follows the system.

The tool windows (Cuts / Layers, Objects, Laser, Move, Console, Material, Camera and others) can be arranged freely: Drag a tab onto another tab header to put the windows together as tabs. Drag it onto the top or bottom edge of a group to place it above or below. Drag it onto the left edge, next to the tools toolbar, to dock it on the left. Drag it onto the workspace to make it a floating window. ⇥ or a double-click on its header docks it again. The dividers between windows can be dragged. ▾ or a double-click on a header collapses a group, × on a tab hides the window. The Window menu shows and hides all windows and bars.

Open Window → Toolbars, or right-click a toolbar shell, to customize the existing toolbars: add or remove available items, reorder them, insert separators and choose the icon size. The Numeric Edits and Text toolbars also use this layout system; their fields still edit the same feature values. Drag a toolbar's grip to move it, dock it at any of the four edges or float it inside the app. The edge determines its orientation: horizontal at the top/bottom, vertical at the sides. Floating bars keep their last orientation. Drop near a row boundary to insert a new row between existing rows. Adjust the number of rows or columns inside a bar in the customizer; content that does not fit scrolls internally. Other bars and the workspace settle over 150 ms, unless reduced motion is enabled. Button groups take one slot. Click the primary button to use the current action; open the group with ▾, a right-click or a 350 ms hold on the primary button. Drag the open group's grip to detach it. The detached group and its source share the current choice; opening it again raises the existing detached group. Its × returns it to the source toolbar. Hiding the source toolbar also hides its detached groups; showing it restores them. Lock toolbar layout prevents layout changes and is saved globally (off by default). A completed drop is saved immediately. Esc, loss of window focus or pointer cancellation cancels a move or tear-off without saving it. Reset toolbar layout restores positions, orientation, rows/columns and visibility and returns detached groups, keeping contents and icon sizes. It does not delete numeric, text or other feature values. Reset all contents restores built-in contents and group choices, preserving custom bars/groups, positions and icon sizes. Restore defaults restores the selected toolbar's contents and its built-in groups' original members. Shared groups update in every toolbar that uses them. Create, rename or delete your own bars in the customizer; built-in bars cannot be deleted. Indent an action under the preceding action to create a flat button group. Built-in and custom groups support the same member editing: add/remove, indent/outdent and reorder. Feature-control sections are not action groups. Floating toolbars stay inside the app, not in separate OS windows. Workspace profiles and icon/font redesign are not included. Window → Reset Windows and Toolbars brings back the initial layout.

Zoom with the mouse wheel and pan with the space bar or the middle mouse button. Panning by dragging with the right mouse button can be switched on under Edit → Settings → Mouse and keyboard. See Keyboard shortcuts for all keys.

File → Transfer Settings … exports settings, devices, material library, library, templates, extensions and interface layout (each selectable) into one .kzs file. Keep it as a backup, or import it on another computer and choose whether to merge or replace. Camera calibrations are only included if you choose them.

The desktop app can also sync these settings through a folder you choose, such as iCloud Drive, Dropbox, Nextcloud, OneDrive or a network drive. Each computer writes only its own file into the "KizamuBeam" subfolder, so no conflicting copies appear. For each entry, the newest change wins, and deletions are synced too.
The desktop app checks for new versions and offers to install them. Under Edit → Settings → General → Update channel you choose Stable or Nightly (nightly builds and release candidates).

Everything you draw in KizamuBeam is an editable vector shape. This page covers the drawing tools, selecting and transforming, and node editing. Combining and reshaping paths is described in Paths and shapes, exact placement in Snapping, guides and measuring.

The drawing tools are on the tools toolbar on the left and in the Tools menu. Tool Shortcut How to use it Lines and curves Ctrl+L Click to set corners; click and drag to make a Bézier curve. Clicking the start point closes the shape; double-click, Enter or right-click finishes. Arc Set the center, then radius and start angle, then end angle — or click start, through point and end (3-point). Shift snaps angles to 15°, Enter commits, Esc discards the arc. Mode and direction are in the tool options; in center mode the direction picks the complementary arc, in 3-point mode it reverses the node order, so the cut starts at the last point. Freehand / Pencil Drag a stroke; it is fitted to smooth, editable curves when you release the mouse. Tool options set the tolerance and whether the stroke is closed. Shaper Drag a gesture: encircling shapes unites them, a line crossing one shape subtracts along the stroke, a closed gesture creates a recognized basic shape (rectangle, rounded rectangle, ellipse, polygon) when recognition is on — otherwise the stroke is fitted like the Pencil. Options: close distance (the ring at the start point shows whether the contour closes on release), smoothing, total cut width and the list of shape suggestions incl. Freehand. The last operation stays adjustable until the next gesture, a tool change or Undo. Rectangle Ctrl+R Drag a rectangle. Shift draws a square, Ctrl draws from the centre. Corner radius in the numeric edits toolbar. Ellipse Ctrl+E Drag an ellipse. Shift draws a circle, Ctrl draws from the centre. Polygon Drag from the centre. Number of corners and Star in the numeric edits toolbar. Text Ctrl+T See Text and codes. Rectangles, ellipses, polygons and text stay editable as such: the corner radius, the number of corners or the text can be changed later. Convert to Path (Ctrl+Shift+C) turns them into ordinary paths.

Click selects an object, Shift+click adds or removes one. Marquee to the right selects objects that lie completely inside, marquee to the left also those it only crosses. Lasso selection (Tools → Path): draw around objects to select those you enclose completely. Shift adds, Ctrl toggles. Ctrl+A selects everything on the current page; Esc clears the selection. A right-click opens a context menu with the commands that fit what is under the pointer: shapes, images, nodes or empty canvas. When many objects lie on top of each other, Tools → Isolate selection helps: only the selected objects can be clicked and snapped to, everything else stays visible but out of reach. A badge at the top shows that isolation is active. Isolation does not affect the job; everything is still lasered. Leave it with Leave isolation or Esc.

Drag a selection to move it. Arrow keys move it by 1 mm (Shift 10 mm, Alt 0.1 mm). Drag a handle to scale. Shift switches between proportional and free scaling, Ctrl scales from the centre. Click the selection a second time (or drag just outside a corner) to rotate. The pivot can be moved. Shift snaps to 15°, Ctrl to 5°, Esc cancels. . and , rotate by 90°. Ctrl+Shift+H and Ctrl+Shift+V mirror.

The numeric edits toolbar at the top shows position, size and rotation of the selection. A 9-point anchor sets which point the values refer to. The fields accept formulas and units, for example 100/3, 2in or 25.4*3, and project parameters such as {Width}/2 (see Templates and library).

Ctrl+G groups, Ctrl+U ungroups. With several objects selected, L R T B align left, right, top and bottom, C and E align centres. The alignment button group in the main toolbar also distributes objects evenly. Arrange → Stacking order brings objects to the front or sends them to the back. Arrays, nesting and pattern fills are described in Arranging and repeating.

Choose Edit nodes (Ctrl+`) to change the shape of paths. With several paths or shapes selected, the nodes of all of them can be edited together. Action How Select nodes Click, Shift+click, marquee (or Node lasso) or Ctrl+A Move nodes Drag them, or nudge with the arrow keys Delete node D or Delete Insert node I, or double-click a segment Segment as line / curve L / C Node as corner / smooth E / S Break the path at the node B Trim the edge back to the intersections T Deleting a segment splits the path there. Every operation is one undo step.

Ctrl+Z undoes, Ctrl+Y (or Ctrl+Shift+Z) redoes. The History window (next to Objects) lists the last 200 changes by name, such as “Move” or “Offset”; click a row to jump several steps back or forward at once.

File → Import (Ctrl+I), drag and drop or paste (Ctrl+V) brings in PNG, JPG, BMP, GIF, WebP and TIFF images. The size comes from the resolution stored in the file (254 DPI if none is given); oversized images are scaled down to the bed. An image sits on a layer like every other object. Speed, power, passes, line interval and the other laser settings come from the layer; double-click the image to open the layer settings with their Image section.

Each image has its own Image Mode, which decides how grey tones become laser dots. The workspace shows the result at laser resolution. Mode Good for Threshold Logos and line art: everything darker than the threshold is lasered. Ordered Even, regular dot pattern. Floyd-Steinberg, Atkinson, Stucki, Jarvis Photos. Error-diffusion dithering with different looks; Atkinson keeps more contrast, Stucki and Jarvis give finer transitions. Newsprint A round dot per screen cell whose size follows the brightness, with adjustable cells per inch and screen angle. Halftone Classic halftone look. Sketch Turns edges into dark strokes and leaves even areas blank. Grayscale Varies the power between Min and Max Power of the layer; for materials that darken evenly. Negative Image inverts the image, for example for dark materials that turn light when lasered.

Tools → Image → Adjust Image … sets brightness, contrast, gamma, sharpening (with radius) and denoise, with a preview, a comparison with the original and a 1:1 view. Adjustments and image mode can be saved as named presets. Save Processed Bitmap … saves the image as PNG exactly as it would be lasered.

Tools → Image → Remove Background … (or Remove BG … in the toolbar) works locally, without a cloud service. The background colours are taken from the image border, or you click them in the preview (Shift+click adds more). Colours within the tolerance become transparent and are not lasered. Clean-up removes small specks and fills small holes; Crop to subject trims the image.

Select an image and one or more closed shapes: Tools → Image → Crop image trims the image to the bounding box of the shape. Tools → Image → Apply mask to image keeps only the inside of the shapes (text works too); the rest becomes transparent. The image keeps its position and resolution; Ctrl+Z undoes both.

Tools → Image → Trace Image … (Alt+T) turns an image into vector paths, with a live preview. Set the threshold, ignore small specks and choose the smoothing. The result is Bézier paths with preserved corners. The type Centerlines traces strokes along their middle as open paths. That is the right choice for handwriting, signatures and line drawings that should be scored as a single line instead of cut around. After tracing, Simplify / smooth paths reduces the number of nodes if needed.

File → Import … (Ctrl+I), dragging files onto the workspace, or pasting with Ctrl+V from other programs all work the same way. Colours are mapped to the nearest palette colour, which means the nearest layer, and several objects arrive as a group.

Paths (including arcs), rectangles, circles, ellipses, lines, polygons, use references, transforms, CSS classes and embedded images. The size comes from width, height and viewBox. Text in SVG files is skipped: convert text to paths in your drawing program before saving.

Lines, polylines with arcs, circles, arcs, ellipses, splines and blocks, with the units stored in the file and true colours. Single lines that touch are joined into continuous paths, so a contour drawn from many segments can be cut as one shape.

Paths stay Bézier curves; RGB, CMYK, grey and spot colours map to layers; embedded images come along. Text becomes outlines from the fonts embedded in the file. Fonts that are not embedded are taken from your system or the font manager; if one is missing, KizamuBeam says which one was replaced. The first PDF page lands on the current page, every further page on a new project page. Illustrator files from version 9 onwards work, because they contain a PDF version. PDFs that are only protected against editing can be imported; files that need a password to open cannot.

.lbrn2 files can be opened (File → Open, as a new project) or imported into the current project. Shapes, groups, images with their adjustments and positions are kept. Layers take over name, mode, speed, power, passes, output, order, fill and image settings, sub-layers, perforation, lead-ins, overcut, power ramp and Z settings. Text stays editable text when the font is installed; otherwise its outlines are kept as a path. Elements that could not be imported are listed in the status bar and in the design check. LightBurn material libraries (.clb) can be imported in the material library.
STL and OBJ files become layered or rib models made of flat parts. KizamuBeam asks which one you want; see Generators.
See Images and tracing.

File → Export (also as toolbar buttons): Format What is exported SVG The current page, with images. DXF The current page in mm, one DXF layer per used layer with name and colour. Curves are exported as exact splines. Images cannot go into DXF. PDF All pages, each at bed size 1:1, every layer as its own PDF layer, fill layers filled, images embedded. Illustrator (.ai) The same PDF-compatible file; opens in Illustrator, Inkscape and Affinity. Texts are exported as outlines.

Laser → Save GCode … writes the job of the current page for the selected device, exactly as it would be sent to the laser, including custom G-code scripts of the device. Use this to run jobs from an SD card or another sender.

File → Transfer Settings … exports settings, devices, material library, library, templates, extensions and window layout into one .kzs file, as a backup or for another computer. See Customizing and settings.

Every object belongs to a layer, and every layer has a colour from the palette at the bottom (00–29, plus the tool layers T1 and T2). Click a colour in the palette to put the selection on that layer. The layer holds all laser settings. Objects, including images, never carry their own speed or power: to laser something differently, put it on another layer. That way a layer is one operation of the job, and the same settings apply to everything on it. The Cuts / Layers window lists the layers that are in use, with mode, speed, power, air assist and output. Values can be edited right in the table; drag rows to change the order in which the layers are lasered.

Mode What happens Line The laser follows the outlines: cutting and scoring. Fill Closed shapes are engraved line by line (or in rings with offset fill). Open lines are skipped. Images can sit on any layer. The table then shows “+ Image”, and the layer dialog gets an Image section with line interval and image settings. Each image keeps its own image mode (see Images and tracing); speed and power come from the layer.
T1 and T2 are never lasered. Use them for construction lines, the outline of a workpiece, camera images to trace, or the path of a text on a path you do not want to cut.

Output decides whether a layer is lasered at all. Hidden layers and objects are still lasered if their output is on; KizamuBeam warns you about that before the job. In the Objects window single objects can be set to Don’t laser: they stay visible (faded) but are not lasered, not written to G-code and not checked.
Double-click a layer to open its Cut Settings. Which fields appear depends on the mode.

Setting Meaning Speed (mm/min) Feed rate while the laser is on. Max Power (%) / Min Power (%) The layer’s power. Min Power is used where power is lowered: in power ramps and for the lightest tones of grayscale images. Passes How often the layer is repeated. Air Assist Switches air assist (M8 or M7) on for this layer. Z offset (mm) and Deeper per pass (mm) Only with a motorized Z axis: move the focus relative to the start height, and go deeper with each pass. Material Links the layer to an entry of the material library; also used by the 3D view and the fit calibration.

Setting Meaning Kerf Offset (mm) Moves the cut outward on outer contours and inward on holes, so parts keep their nominal size. Usually half the kerf width. Tabs Leaves small bridges uncut so parts do not fall out: count per shape or spacing, tab size, optionally skip inner shapes. Perforation Cuts a given length, then leaves a gap, for tear-off edges or fold lines. Lead-in / Lead-out A straight line at an angle or an arc into and out of the contour, always on the waste side, so the start point leaves no mark on the part. Overcut (mm) Continues past the start point to make sure the contour is closed. Power ramp Lowers the power toward corners (from a set change of direction) to avoid burn marks, optionally at the start and end of each cut too. Duplicate lines Removes lines that lie on top of each other before cutting, so nothing is cut twice.

Setting Meaning Line interval (mm) or Lines per inch Distance between the fill lines. Scan angle (°) Direction of the lines: 0° horizontal, 90° vertical. Crosshatch A second pass rotated by 90°. Bi-directional Lasers in both directions (faster). Overscan (%) Runs past the edges with the laser off, so the head is at full speed when it fires. Avoids darker edges. Fill style Line by line, or Offset fill: rings that follow the outline inward. Defaults resets the fields to the defaults of the selected mode.

+ Sub-layer adds further operations on the same shapes, each with its own mode, speed, power, passes and settings. A classic use is “fill, then cut the outline” on a single layer. Sub-layers run after the layer itself and can be switched off one by one.
Appearance in 3D sets how the layer’s parts look in the 3D view: 21 materials from plywood to slate, acrylic and anodized aluminium, each with an optional own colour.
The Material window stores proven settings per material and thickness and applies them to a layer with one click. See Materials and tests.

This page covers everything that happens after the design is done. How to connect a laser for the first time is described in Connecting a laser. The machine windows sit on the right by default: Laser (job, status, devices), Move (jogging and origin) and Console.

Laser → Preview … (Alt+P) simulates the job before anything moves: playback with a time slider, travel moves, and shading by power, a time estimate that takes acceleration and corners into account, the same order as the real job. Start Here lasers the job from the position of the time slider, for example after an abort. The head moves there with the laser off and continues with the power, speed and air assist of that layer.

Frame traces the rectangle around the job, Contour Frame follows its outline. Both can run with a low-power laser so you can see the frame on the material. Use framing to check that the job fits on the workpiece before you start.

Start sends the job. During the job, the Laser window shows progress, elapsed and remaining time. Pause holds the machine; Resume continues. Stop stops the job and resets the controller. The position is kept. Cut Selected Graphics lasers only the selected objects. Before every job and every frame, KizamuBeam checks that all moves, including overscan, stay inside the work area of the machine. If the controller has not reported its origin yet (or never does, as with Marlin), a warning shows the extent of the job and must be confirmed.

The Start From setting in the Laser window decides where the job lands: Start From Meaning Absolute Coords The job is placed exactly where it is on the workspace. The workspace is the machine bed. Needs homing. User Origin The job starts at an origin you set with the Move window. Current Position The job starts where the head is now. With User Origin and Current Position, the job origin (nine points: corners, edge centres, centre) says which point of the job sits at that position.

Adjust in the Laser window changes power and speed in steps of 1 and 10 % (from 10 to 200 %) and rapid moves at 25, 50 or 100 %, while the job runs. Air assist can be switched on and off at once, also during a job. This works with GRBL, grblHAL and FluidNC.

The Laser window has three options for the order of the cuts. Layers are always lasered in the order of the layer table. Option Effect Inner shapes first Holes and inner contours are cut before their outer contour, so parts do not drop before their holes are cut. Reduce travel moves The nearest shape is cut next. When off, the stacking order from the Objects window is used (manual order). Keep groups together Shapes of the same object or group are preferably cut one after another. To choose where a single cut starts and in which direction, use the start point tool (see Paths and shapes).

The Move window jogs the head in steps, sets and clears the user origin, unlocks the machine after an alarm, homes it and moves the head: Move Laser to Selection moves the head to the selected objects. Move Laser to Click: while this button is active, every click on the workspace moves the head there with the laser off. Esc ends the mode.
The Console shows the messages of the controller and lets you send commands, with a history. Alarms and active inputs (limit switches, door, probe) are explained in plain language.
Laser → Save GCode … writes the job to a file, for example to run it from an SD card or from another program.

Each laser is a device with its own connection, work area and settings. Pick the device at the top of the Laser window, or manage them under Laser → Device → Devices …. New devices can start from templates for common lasers; the list is grouped by manufacturer, with generic templates per controller at the end. Models sold with several laser modules have one entry per module. Below the list you see the selected template's laser module, work area, equipment and where the values come from; check the work area before the first job. The laser module (type, optical power, wavelength) can also be entered later in the device settings. Laser → Device → Device Settings … holds, among others: work area, S value for 100 % power, baud rate, network address, rapid speed and acceleration (Read from Machine fetches them from FluidNC or GRBL), receive buffer size, limit switches (with "None", KizamuBeam never homes by itself and asks before homing), motorized Z axis (for Z offsets per pass and the focus test), air assist command (M8 or M7), G-code scripts: commands to run before and after every job, red-dot pointer: the offset between beam and pointer, so framing and click moves can aim with the red dot, FluidNC extras (see below).

With a FluidNC controller, Laser → FluidNC offers: Run job from the SD card or flash: upload the job first and run it there, so a Wi-Fi dropout does not stop it. Pause and stop work as usual. Files on the controller: list, upload, run and delete files. Configuration …: read, search and change the config.yaml, try values out or save them, and restart. Every save keeps a backup of the previous state (the last ten per device), which you can restore. Outputs: free outputs (for example a fume extractor) can be switched in the Laser window and turned on automatically during every job.

KizamuBeam works with FluidNC, GRBL 1.1, grblHAL, Marlin and Smoothieware. Buttons for homing, jogging, origin and console adapt to the controller. See Machine compatibility for details and tested lasers.
Engraving cylinders: see Rotary. Running a laser that is connected to another computer: see Remote control. Trying everything without a laser: see Virtual Machine.

Good results depend on the right speed, power and focus for each material. KizamuBeam helps you find these values with test patterns and keeps them in a material library, so you only have to find them once.

The Material window stores cut settings per material and thickness, optionally with the image settings too. To use an entry, select a layer and apply the entry to it; the layer takes over all its settings. Save: set up a layer the way you like it and save it as a new entry (material, thickness, title). Exchange: export and import entries as .kzm files. Older .lwm files still import, and LightBurn libraries (.clb) are imported as far as their fields have an equivalent. Extensions can add material entries too (see Templates, library and extensions). Material entries also carry the 3D look and the results of a fit calibration.

Laser → Tests and Calibration → Material Test … (or the Toolbox → Laser and Calibration) creates a grid of test cells with two stepped values, for example speed in the rows and power in the columns, with labels. Each cell gets its own test layer. The test does not change your document: send it straight to the laser with Preview, Frame, Start or Save G-code in the dialog. The cells run in order of increasing energy, so a test you stop early has done the gentle cells. Typical uses: Engraving: find the speed and power that give the darkness you want without burning. Cutting: find the fastest speed that still cuts through (set passes in the dialog). Scoring: find a line that is visible but does not go deep.

Laser → Tests and Calibration → Evaluate Material Test … (or Evaluate Photo … in the test dialog) helps you read the result: Take a picture with the connected camera, or open a photo (from a phone, for example). Click the four corners of the cell grid. With a calibrated camera and absolute start, the grid is placed automatically. Click the best cell in the photo, and apply its values to the active layer or save them to the material library. KizamuBeam measures how dark each cell is against the bare material in the gaps, and for engravings suggests the cell that is almost as dark as the darkest one with the least energy. Whether a cell burned too much or cut through is still for you to judge.
