documents.t: Laser → Tests and Calibration → Focus Test … helps you find the right distance between laser head and material. Ramp works with every laser. Tilt the material on a shim, laser one long line with height marks underneath, then click the sharpest spot in the dialog. KizamuBeam tells you how far the focus is off. Z series needs a motorized Z axis. It lasers a row of short lines, each at a different Z offset. Click the sharpest one to enter its offset on the layer or move Z there directly. Like the material test, the focus test never touches your document.

Slot-together parts only fit when kerf and clearance are right. Laser → Tests and Calibration → Calibrate Fit … (also in the Toolbox and in the Material window) creates test parts on a new page: a 20 × 20 mm square to measure the kerf, a slot comb with stepped slot widths, a hole plate with a tab comb with stepped clearance. The numbers are engraved on a separate layer. After lasering, measure the square and enter it, together with the number of the best-fitting tab and slot. KizamuBeam computes the kerf, the clearance per side and the slot allowance and stores them with the material in the library. A kerf offset on the layer is taken into account. From then on, new boxes, drawers, inserts and shelves take thickness, kerf and clearance from the calibration of the layer's material, and the Joint tool proposes matching values. Existing parts get a button to apply the calibrated values, and the design check compares joints against the calibration.

Window → Notes keeps notes on the material (type, thickness, source), the setup (focus, bed, origin, how the piece is held) and the processing (order, passes, finishing, what to change next time). The notes are saved in the project file and in templates, so the next run starts with what you learned.

The Objects window (on the right below the layers; Window → Objects) shows all objects of the current page as a tree: pages, layers, objects and expandable groups, with the frontmost object on top. A click selects an object, Shift or Ctrl adds more. The selection on the workspace follows along. Double-click a name to rename an object or a layer. Eye: hide an object or layer. Lock: the object can no longer be selected on the workspace. Laser icon: Don’t laser. The object stays visible (drawn faded, struck through in the list) but is not lasered, not written to G-code and not checked. Handy for parts that are already cut or kept for later. On a layer row, the same icon switches the whole layer’s output. Drag rows to change the stacking order, move objects to another layer or reorder layers. A right-click opens a context menu with Rename, Zoom to Selection, Hide, Move to layer, Move to page and the usual editing commands. Hidden or locked objects can be shown and unlocked there.

With Absolute Coords as the start mode, anything that lies completely outside the work area is skipped without a warning, as long as something else is on the bed. This lets you keep spare parts next to the bed. Parts that stick out partly are still reported.

A project can have several pages, for example one per material or sheet. Pages are listed at the top of the Objects window and in the Pages menu; Page Up and Page Down switch between them. Each page has its own objects; the layer settings apply to the whole project. Drawing, lasering and SVG, DXF or G-code export work on the current page. PDF and AI export contain all pages. Add, duplicate, rename (double-click), delete and reorder pages by dragging. Drag objects onto a page row to move them there, or use Pages → Move Selection to Next Page. Nesting and generators create new pages by themselves when parts do not fit.

Several projects can be open at once, as tabs above the workspace. Each tab has its own pages, selection, view and undo history. File → New (Ctrl+N) or + opens an empty tab. Open and New from template use a new tab unless the current one is empty. Ctrl+Tab and Ctrl+Shift+Tab switch tabs; drag to reorder; × or a middle-click closes a tab. Unsaved changes are marked with •. Copy and paste works between tabs. All open tabs are backed up automatically and come back after a restart.
File → Save (Ctrl+S) stores the project as a .kzb file. Images, cut settings, pages, notes and parameters are all inside, so the file can be passed on as it is. Older .lwk files still open.

The History window (tab next to Objects) lists the last 200 changes by name, with the time. Click a row to jump several steps back or forward. Undone steps stay greyed out below the current state until a new change discards them.

Window → Notes keeps notes with the project, in three fields: Material: type, thickness, where you bought it. Setup: focus, bed, origin, how the piece is held. Processing: order, passes, finishing, what to change next time. The notes are saved in the project file and in templates.

KizamuBeam’s shape tools always return clean Bézier curves: corners and straight segments are kept, and rounded parts are fitted with at most 0.02 mm deviation. Results stay editable like anything you draw.

Select two or more shapes and choose one of the operations under Tools → Boolean Operations or in the button group of the main toolbar: Operation Shortcut Result Weld (union) Alt++ Merges the shapes into one outline. On a single group or text, it merges its overlapping parts. Boolean Difference Alt+- Cuts one shape out of the others. Boolean Intersection Alt+* Keeps only the area where the shapes overlap. Boolean Options (in the button group or under Tools → Boolean Operations) set which shape is the base (first selected, backmost or frontmost) and whether the originals are kept. The same menu also has Subtract front from back and Subtract back from front. Good to know: Shapes in a group count as one area, so overlaps inside a group do not turn into holes. Texts and groups are treated as outlines automatically. Open lines, such as living hinge cuts, are trimmed exactly at subtracted shapes. Images are left out.

Offset Shapes (Alt+O) draws a new outline at a given distance, outward, inward or both, with round, sharp or beveled corners and a live preview. Open lines get a closed outline around them. Typical uses: a border around text, a backing plate, or an inlay pocket.

Tools → Warp … bends the selection over its frame: arc, arc upper, arc lower, bulge, flag or vanishing-point perspective, from −100 to 100 %, optionally rotated by 90°. Shapes, text and images are warped together. Shapes and text become Bézier paths, images are recalculated at their original resolution.

Under Tools → Path: Close path closes open paths whose ends are at most 0.5 mm apart. Close paths with tolerance … goes up to 20 mm and shows how many shapes will be closed. Auto-join selected shapes (Alt+J) joins open paths whose ends meet (within 0.05 mm) into one path. Break apart (Alt+B) splits paths, shapes and texts into their individual lines and curves. Trim shapes (Ctrl+K): hover over a curve, the piece up to the next intersections turns red and is removed with a click. The remaining pieces are joined at the intersections, so two overlapping circles become one outline after two clicks. Ctrl+click does not join, Shift+click keeps the removed piece. Set start point: click a node to make the cut start there, or click an edge to insert a new start node. That node is removed again when you move or reset the start point, unless you have edited it. Shift+click reverses the direction. While the tool is active, all start points, directions, lead-ins and lead-outs are shown on the workspace exactly as the job will cut them. Reverse direction flips the cut direction. Mark centers adds a small cross at the centre of every circle and arc, for centre punching or drilling.

Tools → Extract outer contour and islands … derives the outer silhouette of the selected objects, optionally with chosen inner areas, for example as a backing plate. Tools → Path → Separate path islands … splits a path made of several separate pieces into independent objects; each piece keeps its own holes. Tools → Path → Edit freehand path … continues an open path at one of its ends or redraws a section between two nodes by hand. Tools → Local contour offset … moves only part of a contour outward or inward.

Tools → Path → Round or chamfer corners … rounds corners of any vector shape with an exact radius, rounds them inward or chamfers them. In the node editor it works on the selected nodes, otherwise on all corners of the selected shapes. If an edge is too short, the radius is reduced.

Tools → Simplify / smooth paths … refits the selected paths with fewer nodes, as curves or as straight lines, within a tolerance in mm. Sharp corners can be kept. An orange preview shows the result before you apply it. This is useful for traced images and imported files with many nodes.

Snap in the status bar switches snapping on and off. Objects and the pointer snap to nodes, midpoints, centres, intersections, lines and quadrant points of circles. Grid in the status bar snaps to the grid. Ctrl while dragging switches snapping off (or on) for the moment. Alt while dragging snaps more strongly and shows alignment guides on other objects. Circles and arcs are also recognised inside paths, for example holes in a plate or imported DXF circles, so their true centre snaps. View → Show centers shows centre crosses always, for the selection only, or not at all.

View → Grid shows or hides the grid. Under Grid Settings … you set the spacing (e.g. 25.4 for inches), subdivisions, every nth line bold, colour and opacity, and optionally use the finest spacing as the snap grid.

Drag a guide out of the top ruler (horizontal) or the left ruler (vertical). Guides lie on their own Guides layer: they are never lasered or exported, and Ctrl+A, the palette and shape operations leave them alone. Drag a guide to move it, or back into the ruler to delete it. The Guides layer can be hidden and locked in the Objects window. Guides apply to all pages.
Tools → Measure (or the ruler button): click a start and an end point, with snapping. KizamuBeam shows length, Δx, Δy and angle; over a circle, diameter and radius. Esc clears the measurement.

Arrange → Relations (or the relations button group on the tools toolbar) moves or turns one object so that it relates to another. Click the reference first (it stays), then the element of the object that should adapt. Relation What it does Concentric Two circles, ellipses or polygons share a centre (also holes inside paths). Equal size Same radius for two circles, same length for two edges. Parallel / Perpendicular The second object turns by the smallest angle. Horizontal / Vertical Turns one edge level or upright. Tangent The second object moves until it touches. Distance Asks for a distance between edges, points or circles. Relations are applied once, like a command; each is one undo step.

For parts that must keep exact dimensions while you change them, use Toolbox → Sketches with relations → New sketch (or Convert to sketch). In a sketch, lines, rectangles, circles and arcs keep their relations and dimensions permanently, like in a CAD program. Relations from the bar at the top or by key: coincident (O), horizontal (H), vertical (V), parallel (P), perpendicular (N), equal (E), tangent (T), concentric (X), midpoint (M), symmetric (Y), fixed (F). Dimension (D): a line gets a length, two lines an angle, a circle a diameter, an arc a radius, two points a distance. Double-click a dimension to change it. Dimensions can be formulas with project parameters, such as Width / 2. Colours: blue = still free, dark = fully defined, red = conflict. Construction geometry (G) is drawn dashed and never lasered. Double-click reopens a sketch, Enter or Done closes it, Cancel discards all changes since opening.

Print and Cut cuts out a printed sheet exactly along the print, for example stickers or cardboard figures. Start it from the Toolbox → Laser and Calibration → Print and Cut. Place marks: put three registration marks around the design (or turn your own objects into marks). The marks are printed and exported, but never lasered. Print the design at actual size (100 %, no "fit to page"). Measure: put the sheet in the laser. For each mark, move the head to its centre with a low-power laser dot and the jog buttons, or click it in the camera image. Align: KizamuBeam moves and rotates the whole design onto the print. With three marks it also corrects printer scaling and skew. The remaining error is shown. Frame and start as usual. Two marks are enough to move and rotate; three also correct distortion from the printer.

A jig is a holding plate with cut-outs for a batch of identical workpieces, such as keychain blanks or coasters. Create it in the Toolbox → Copy and Arrange → Jig. The slot shapes can come from: selected objects (any imported vector file, shapes or text), a traced photo or scan (enter the real width), pieces detected on the bed with the calibrated camera. A jig can hold several kinds of workpieces, each with count and 0° or 90° rotation. The generator sets the clearance per side (kerf included), slot spacing, finger notches to take the pieces out, engraved slot numbers and three engraved registration marks. The plate fits the slots or has a fixed size. Double-click the jig later to change everything.

Cut the jig and leave it in the laser (or put it back later). Place your design on slot 1, for example a name. Choose Toolbox → Copy and Arrange → Place on jig slots and enter the slots, such as 1-5, 8. A copy goes into every chosen slot, at the same position within the slot. Variable text counts up per slot (serial number or table row), and the jig itself is hidden so only the design is cut. If you remove the jig and put it back, measure its engraved marks with Print and Cut: the jig and all copies are aligned together. For workpieces lying anywhere on the bed, see Place on workpieces.

The laser often stands in the workshop, while you design at your desk. With remote control, the computer next to the laser runs KizamuBeam in host mode, and other computers use that laser as if it were connected to them.

On the computer that is connected to the laser: Connect the laser as usual (see Connecting a laser). Choose Laser → Remote control → Host mode … and switch host mode on. It is off by default. Optionally tick Confirm remote job starts on this computer, so every remote start has to be confirmed at the laser. The host listens on port 47900. The connection is encrypted.

On the other computer: Add a device (Laser → Device → Devices …) with the connection Other KizamuBeam (network). Click Find host … to find hosts in the network, or enter the host's address (over a VPN such as Tailscale or WireGuard, enter it by hand). Click Pair …. The host shows a 6-digit code; type it in on this computer. The host lists all paired computers and can remove them or change their role: Role May Operator move, frame, start, pause and stop Viewer only watch status, progress and console

Start does not send G-code. It sends the project (layers, cut settings, images) and the fonts it uses. The host computes the job with its own device settings and runs it over its own connection. Before the laser starts, you see the host's preview, the estimated time and any warnings (work area, missing fonts, air assist). Frame, contour frame, material test, focus test and the setup test job work the same way. Jogging, homing, console, overrides, pause and stop go straight to the host's machine. Status and progress reach every connected computer, and a network dropout never interrupts a running job: the host keeps going. Whoever stands at the host can always pause or stop. A remote start is refused while the host's machine is busy or not connected. Start Here and raw G-code from the client are not possible yet.

Laser → Remote control → Remote jobs … on the host lists the last 20 received jobs with preview, sender and time. Start one again (it is computed anew with the current settings) or Open in editor as a normal project.

Laser → Remote control → Take over from host … copies the host's device settings onto your device (name and connection stay), merges the host's material library and adds the host's cameras with their calibration. The camera image then comes through the connection, a few frames per second.
documents.s: Taking over settings from the host

documents.t: A rotary turns a round object under the laser, so you can engrave cups, glasses, bottles or rolling pins. KizamuBeam converts the Y direction of your design into rotation of the object.

Open Laser → Device → Rotary Setup … (or Rotary … in the Laser window). The settings are stored per device: Setting Meaning Enable rotary Switches rotary mode on for this device. Rollers / Chuck Rollers: the object rests on driven rollers. Chuck: the object is clamped and turned directly. Axis Y (rotary connected instead of the Y motor), or a separate A, B, C or Z axis. Travel per rotation How far the axis moves (in mm or degrees, usually 360°) for one full turn of the roller or chuck. Roller diameter Diameter of the driven roller (rollers only). Object diameter Measured at the widest point of the engraving. You can enter the circumference instead, for example measured with a tape. Reverse direction Flips the rotation if the design comes out mirrored. Test rotation turns the object exactly once with the values entered. If it turns too far or not far enough, change the travel per rotation in the same ratio.

When the rotary is on: the design's Y direction becomes rotation, and the speed is adjusted so the speed on the surface is right, this applies to jobs, images, frame, Move and Start Here, only X is checked against the bed, and KizamuBeam warns when the design is taller than the object's circumference, with a separate axis, the axis is set to zero at the start (G92 A0, or B, C, Z), and the frame returns to the start afterwards, with the rotary on the Y port, KizamuBeam asks before homing (homing would turn the rotary).

Cups and many glasses are thinner at the bottom than at the top. Enter the object diameter at the left and the right edge of the job. The rotation then follows the diameter at each X position, so the engraving keeps its true size, and the middle of the job stays straight. With rollers, KizamuBeam assumes the object rests on its thicker end.

Place the design so its height (Y) is not larger than the circumference of the object (diameter × π). Focus on the highest point of the object, directly under the head. Do a frame first: the head moves along X and the object turns. Write the object diameter into the project notes, so the next run is quick.

Window → Parameters holds named values for the whole project: numbers, texts and yes/no values. Use them anywhere: In a text or QR code, {Name} inserts the value. Formulas work too: {Width / 2}, {round(Length; 1)}, {Name + " Ltd"}, {Lid ? "with lid" : ""}. Write {{ and }} for literal braces. In the numeric toolbar (X, Y, width, height, rotation, corner radius, font size and more), you can type a formula instead of a number. A bound field shows its formula in italics; typing a plain number removes the formula. Fields of generators (for example the material thickness of a box) accept a parameter or formula; choice and yes/no fields get one with the ƒ button. Changing a value recalculates everything at once, on all pages. Numbers can have a range and then get a slider. Renaming a parameter renames it in all texts and formulas. Edit → Visible If … shows and lasers an object only while a condition holds, such as Lid or Width > 100. These objects carry a ƒ in the Objects window.

A template is a project with parameters that asks for its values when you use it. File → Save as template … stores the current project as a template (.kzt) with title, description and preview. You decide which parameters are asked, in which order, with which label and whether as a slider. Parameters that are not asked keep their value. File → New from template … shows your templates. Picking one opens it as a new project with a fill-in dialog and a live preview. Cancel goes back to where you were. File → Fill in template … asks the values of the current project again. KizamuBeam includes a key fob (the name shrinks to fit), a name tag (optional second line and holes) and a labelled box (a finger-jointed box with a label on the front). Templates from installed extensions appear under "From extensions". .kzt files can be added with From file … in the template dialog or by dragging them onto the workspace. To change a template, open it with File → Open …, edit it and save it as a template again. In the desktop app the templates live in the templates folder of the settings folder (Show folder opens it).

File → Series from table (CSV) … turns each row of a table into a copy of the current page with the values filled in, for example name tags for a whole class. Set up the design with parameters (for example {Name} in a text). Open the dialog and fill in the table: one column per parameter, one row per copy. You can paste cells from a spreadsheet, or import a CSV file. Choose the layout: a grid starting at the machine origin (continuing on further pages), or one page per row. The copies go onto new pages behind the current one, with the placeholders replaced. Your template page stays editable. The table is saved with the project, so a template can bring its own list. Columns are matched to parameters by name or chosen by hand; numbers may use a decimal comma, and yes/no columns accept 1, yes and x. One undo step. For counters and dates on each job instead of a fixed list, see variable text.

Tools → Toolbox … (also Window → Toolbox and the tile button in the tools toolbar) lists all generators and special tools as tiles, in groups: Mechanics, Boxes and Furniture, 3D slot-together models, Sketches with relations, Joints and Bending, Copy and Arrange, Text and Data, Image, Laser and Calibration. Search looks at names, descriptions and keywords in English and German; Enter starts the first hit. Favourites: right-click a tile to pin it at the top. Below the favourites are the three tools you used last. New tools carry a "NEW" badge until you use them once. If a tool needs a selection, the status bar says what to select.

Window → Library keeps motifs, images and design elements for reuse, with previews, search and tags. + Selection (or Edit → Add to library …) stores the selected objects with name, type and tags. Files …, or dragging SVG, DXF, PDF, AI, image or .kza files onto the window, adds files directly. Double-click an item, or drag it onto the workspace, to insert it as a group. An item on a single layer lands on the current layer. Items can be renamed, retagged and exported as .kza files to share. KizamuBeam comes with 400 built-in items of its own design, ready to cut or engrave: 200 motifs (animals, plants, food, holidays, vehicles, tools, symbols, zodiac, space and more) and 200 design elements (frames, borders, corners, dividers, ornaments, badges, banners, patterns). All are closed vector paths. Built-in items cannot be changed; insert one and save it with + Selection to keep your own version. The library also holds the patterns for pattern fill.

File → Extensions … installs packs (.kzp files) that add device presets, templates, material library entries and library items without a new version of KizamuBeam. A pack contains data only, never program code, and every entry is checked before it is installed. The catalogue in the same window lists the official packs: install or update with one click. The catalogue is signed, and every pack is checked against its checksum. Install … or dragging a .kzp file onto the workspace installs a pack from a file. The dialog lists the content and says whether it is an update. Removing a pack removes its entries again. See the list of extensions for what is available.

Choose the Text tool (Ctrl+T) and click on the workspace to start typing. Drag a box instead of clicking to get a text box with word wrap. Click an existing text to edit it. The text toolbar below the numeric edits toolbar holds all text options: font, height, bold, italic, upper case, letter and line spacing, alignment, maximum width and height, weld, text on path and variable text. Option What it does Weld Merges overlapping letters into one outline, for script fonts or tight letter spacing. Wrap / Max width Breaks lines at word boundaries at the box width; the box grows downward. Dragging the side handles reflows the text. Max. height Scales a block that gets too tall down evenly. Shrink Scales a text that is too wide down instead of condensing it. Text stays editable. Convert to Path (Ctrl+Shift+C) turns it into its real font outlines, for example before node editing.

All fonts installed on your computer can be used. File → Fonts … (or More fonts … at the end of the font list) opens the font manager: Search all Google Fonts with a live preview of your own sample text, filter by kind and sort by popularity or name. Install downloads the font into KizamuBeam, so it works offline and without installing it in the system. Use applies it to the selected text. Import your own TTF or OTF files the same way. Star a font to make it a favourite; favourites appear at the top of the font list. When a project uses a font that is missing on this computer, KizamuBeam offers to download it from Google Fonts.

Select a text and a shape, then choose Tools → Text Functions → Apply Path to Text (or On Path in the text toolbar). The text follows the line, curve, rectangle, ellipse or polygon. In the text toolbar you set the offset along the curve, the distance from the curve and which side the text is on. Text and shape stay linked: if you edit or move the shape, the text follows. The shape is lasered too, unless it is on a tool layer (T1/T2) or hidden. Tools → Text Functions → Remove Path from Text separates them again.

Variable text fills in placeholders when the job is created, for serial numbers, dates or names from a list. Turn on Variable in the text toolbar and use these placeholders: Placeholder Becomes %# Serial number; %4# with leading zeros (0042) %d.%m.%Y, %H:%M … Date and time %0, %1 … or %{Header} Column of a CSV file (comma, semicolon or tab separated) The Variable Text window (Tools → Text Functions → Variable Text …) sets the current number, start, end, step and whether it advances automatically after every job or saved G-code file. The number is also the row of the CSV file. Each object can have its own offset, so one page can hold several consecutive numbers. Bake Variable Text turns the current content into fixed text. For a whole series of pages from a table, see Templates and library.

Open QR code in the Toolbox (or search for it there). Double-click an existing QR code to edit it. A QR code can contain: text or a web address, Wi-Fi access data, a contact card (vCard). Choose the error correction (L, M, Q, H) and the size in mm. Negative Image lasers the background including the quiet zone, for dark materials. The modules are merged into closed outlines, so put the code on a Fill layer to engrave it. Double-click a QR code to edit it.

Toolbox → Text and Data → Barcode creates Code 128, EAN-13, EAN-8, UPC-A, Code 39 and ITF barcodes, with check digits where the format uses them. Set the width and bar height, show the human-readable text below the bars, and reduce the bar width to make up for the beam width. Negative Image lasers the gaps instead of the bars. The dialog warns when bars get too narrow for the laser. QR codes and barcodes accept variable text and project parameters too, for example a serial number as Code 128.

The KizamuBeam Virtual Machine is a separate program (a separate download on the releases page) that behaves like a laser with a FluidNC 3.7 or GRBL 1.1 controller. Use it to learn KizamuBeam, to try a job before you waste material, or to test camera functions without a camera.

Start the Virtual Machine. In KizamuBeam, add a device from the template KizamuBeam Virtual Machine and connect. The Virtual Machine listens on Telnet (port 2323) and WebSocket (port 8181). The ports can be changed, and the machine can optionally be reached from the network. Other programs can connect to it as a GRBL or FluidNC network device.

Top view: the bed with burn marks (darker with more power), rapid moves and the head with the laser spot. 3D view: bed, frame, gantry, laser head and beam. Place workpieces with size, thickness, position and one of the 21 material looks. Every line burns into the material in real time: slower or stronger passes come out darker and deeper, and where the energy is enough, the material is cut through. Parts: as soon as a shape is cut all around, it becomes a loose part. Take it out, turn it over and inspect it. A part that still hangs on a spot that was not cut through is marked orange. State: positions, overrides, planner, run time, connections and a console. The burn model is calibrated to a 10 W diode laser (100 % at 300 mm/min cuts 3 mm plywood). It is a model, not a measurement, so real materials still need a material test.

The Virtual Machine emulates the receive buffer, the motion planner with acceleration, real-time commands (hold, resume, reset, overrides, air assist), homing, jogging, work offsets and alarms. It tells you when a program overfills the receive buffer, and when the head runs into the frame it loses its position like a real machine. Power cycle switches it off and on.

The Virtual Machine renders a camera image of its 3D scene, from above the bed or from the laser head, and serves it like a network camera (MJPEG stream at http://…:8282/stream). In KizamuBeam, add it as a network camera in the Camera window to try calibration, workpiece detection and Print and Cut without hardware.

The Virtual Machine can also answer like a Ruida controller (as used in many CO2 lasers) over UDP. This is meant for testing other programs that speak Ruida; KizamuBeam itself does not support Ruida controllers yet.
The sidebar can be resized, hidden (Ctrl+B, ⌘B on the Mac) and placed left or right. Theme and language are under Settings → View.

Generators create finished parts from a few dimensions instead of drawing them by hand. They are all in the Toolbox (Tools → Toolbox …, Window → Toolbox or the tile button in the tools toolbar), sorted into groups and searchable. Page Generators Gears and racks Gear, gear pair, rack Pulleys and cams Timing pulley, disc cam Finger-jointed boxes Finger Joint Box, Finger Joint Box with Dividers Drawers, inserts and shelves Drawer, divider insert, slot-together shelf Layered and rib models Layered model and rib model from an STL or OBJ file Disc sphere A sphere or lamp shade made of interlocking discs Multi-layer work Your own shapes stacked into a layered relief Joints between your own shapes, the lid hinge, living hinges and slots are tools rather than generators: see Joints, hinges and 3D view. Jigs are described under Print and Cut and jigs, dimensioned sketches under Snapping, guides and measuring.

Every generator dialog shows a live preview and checks the values as you type; problems appear in red or orange below the fields. Rarely needed settings are under Advanced. Create makes the part and closes the dialog. Add makes the part and keeps the dialog open, so you can set up the next one with other values. When you edit an existing part, Add creates a new one and leaves the edited part unchanged. New parts go to the first free spot on the page, starting at the bottom left, 2 mm apart and 3 mm from the edge. Every object on the page is avoided, and an assembly (such as a box) keeps its layout. When the page is full, the part goes onto a new page. A part larger than the work area asks first: Create anyway in the centre, go back, or cancel. Each Create or Add is one undo step.

Generators create parametric parts: they keep their parameters in the project. Double-click a part to reopen its dialog. The outline is recalculated, and position and rotation stay. For an assembly such as a box, a double-click on any panel edits the whole box; parts that are no longer needed disappear and new ones (such as a lid) are added. Some changes would break the parameters: scaling, node editing, or a Boolean operation without "Keep originals". KizamuBeam then asks whether to convert the part to ordinary paths or to edit its parameters instead. Convert to Path does the conversion on purpose.

Every numeric field accepts a project parameter or a formula, for example {Thickness} or {Width} - 2 * {Thickness}. Choice and yes/no fields get a parameter with the ƒ button. That way a box in a template follows the values filled in, and changing the material thickness in one place updates every part.

Most generators have a Kerf field: the width of the laser cut. Outlines are offset outward by half of it and holes and slots get smaller, so parts come out at their nominal size. A kerf offset on the layer is applied on top, so set the kerf in one place only. Slot-together parts also have a Fit clearance: how much play each joint gets (negative values give a press fit). Once the material of the layer is calibrated, new parts take thickness, kerf and clearance from the calibration, and existing parts offer a button to apply it.
The 3D view shows assemblies put together and marks collisions in red. The design check tests the fit of every joint and whether the parts can be assembled in some order.
Find both box generators in Toolbox → Boxes and Furniture. For a lid that opens on a pin, add a lid hinge afterwards.

Field Meaning Dimensions Outside dimensions or Inside dimensions: whether width, depth and height are measured outside or inside the walls. Width, Depth, Height Size of the box in mm. Material thickness Thickness of the board. Measure it; boards are rarely exactly as thick as sold. Up Open, or Closed (lid with fingers). Finger width Minimum finger width. Every edge gets an odd number of equally wide fingers. Fit clearance Every finger gets this much narrower; negative = press fit. Kerf Width of the laser cut; outlines are offset outward by half of it. The front and back walls own the corners. The parts are separate objects in a compact arrangement: identical parts stay together. A double-click on any part edits the whole box, on every page. Parts still in their generated layout move apart when they grow; parts you arranged yourself stay where they are.

Put text or images on a panel and group them with it, or simply place them on top: in the 3D view, engravings show on the panel they lie on. The labelled box template (File → New from template …) is a ready example with a label on the front.

Measure the material thickness with a caliper at several spots and enter the average. Start with a fit clearance of 0 and the kerf of your laser (0.1 to 0.2 mm for a diode laser on plywood). Cut the box. If it is too tight, increase the clearance in steps of 0.05 mm; if it is loose, decrease it. The fit calibration finds these values for a material in one test, and new boxes then take them automatically.

An open or closed box with dividers that cross each other. This generator is experimental: check the parts in the 3D view and on an offcut before cutting the real material. Field Meaning Width, Depth, Height, Material thickness, Up As for the box. Compartments across width / Compartments across depth Number of compartments in each direction. Width distribution / Depth distribution Clear compartment sizes as ratios or in mm, separated by colons. 1:2:1 makes the middle compartment twice as wide; 36mm:1 makes the first one 36 mm and the second takes the rest. + - * / and parentheses work too. Empty = equal compartments. Divider drop below box top How much lower the dividers are than the walls. Kerf Width of the laser cut. Finger width and Fit clearance are under Advanced. Pieces and their holes share one layer.

The Disc sphere (Toolbox → 3D slot-together models) builds a sphere or lamp shade from round discs. The discs hold each other through angled slots, without glue. The discs sit on the face directions of a polyhedron, chosen under Layout. More discs make a rounder sphere with more slots; the icosahedron is the default. Polyhedron Discs Cube 6 Octahedron 8 Dodecahedron 12 Cuboctahedron 14 Icosahedron 20 Rhombicuboctahedron 26 Football 32 Field Meaning Diameter Outer diameter of the finished sphere. Overlap (%) 0 % = the discs just interlock, 100 % = as far as possible without three discs meeting in one point. More overlap gives larger discs, a firmer hold and more pattern. Material thickness Thickness of the material. Top opening Hole in the top disc, for example for a lamp socket (E14 about 30 mm, E27 about 40 mm); 0 = none. Bottom opening Hole in the bottom disc, for example to change the bulb (Advanced). Fit clearance Extra slot width; negative = press fit. Kerf Width of the laser cut. Each pair of crossing discs shares a chord that is split in half: one disc is slotted from one end, the other from the other end. Slots for discs that cross at an angle are made wider accordingly, and sharp corners at the slot entrances get a small chamfer.

Thin, slightly flexible material works best: paper, card, polypropylene or veneer. The discs have to bend a little when the last ones are slotted in. Start with the discs around one point and work your way around the sphere. For a lamp, use LED bulbs only: they stay cool. Keep paper and wood well away from the bulb. The 3D view shows the assembled sphere and checks that the discs do not collide.

These generators build on the finger-jointed box and are in Toolbox → Boxes and Furniture. All of them are assemblies: the 3D view shows them put together, and the tests behind them check that no parts overlap.

A drawer with a carcass open at the front, a matching drawer box and a front panel. Without the carcass you get just the drawer box, for an opening that already exists. Field Meaning Width, Height, Depth Outer size of the carcass. Without carcass: size of the opening. Material thickness Thickness of the board. With carcass Builds the carcass too. Front panel Overlay (covers the carcass), Inset (inside the opening) or None. Handle Hand slot or Round hole, with Handle width (slot length or hole diameter) and Handle height; or None. Side clearance, Top clearance, Back clearance Air between drawer box and carcass. Gap around the front panel The front panel is made this much smaller on every side. Kerf Width of the laser cut. Finger width and Fit clearance are under Advanced.

A grid of halved dividers that slot into each other, for a box or drawer: for screws, beads, tea bags or game pieces. Field Meaning Inner width / Inner depth Inner size of the box or drawer the insert goes into. Divider height Height of the dividers. Material thickness Thickness of the board. Compartments across / Compartments deep Number of compartments in each direction. Fit clearance Slots are made this much wider than the material thickness; negative = press fit. End clearance Dividers are made this much shorter than the inner size so the insert drops in easily. Kerf Width of the laser cut.

Two sides and any number of shelves joined by cross slots: no glue, no screws. Field Meaning Width Length of the shelves. Depth, Height Size of the sides. Material thickness Thickness of the board. 4 mm or more makes a stable shelf. Number of shelves 1 to 30. Lowest shelf above floor Height of the underside of the lowest shelf. Top shelf below top edge Distance from the top of the sides to the top face of the highest shelf. Shelf overhang How far the shelves stick out past the sides. Fit clearance Extra slot width; negative = press fit. Kerf Width of the laser cut. The shelves are evenly spaced between the lowest and the highest one.

The gear generators make real involute teeth, generated the way a hob cuts them, with exact root fillets and undercut for small tooth counts. The outlines are Bézier curves within 0.004 mm of the true shape. Find them in Toolbox → Mechanics.

Field Meaning Number of teeth 5 to 400. Module Pitch diameter divided by the number of teeth. Meshing gears need the same module. The pitch diameter is module × teeth: 24 teeth at module 2 give 48 mm. Pressure angle 20° is common. Meshing gears need the same angle. Backlash Play of the gear pair on the pitch circle; each gear's teeth get thinner by half of it. Kerf Width of the laser cut; the outline is offset outward by half of it, the bore inward. Bore None, Round, D-shaft (flat) with the size across the flat, or With keyway with keyway width and depth. Under Advanced: Profile shift x: positive values make the tooth roots stronger and avoid undercut on small gears; the centre distance changes by x × module. Root fillet and Bottom clearance (× module): standard values are 0.38 and 0.25. Backlash and kerf are separate on purpose: backlash makes room between the teeth of two gears, the kerf makes up for the material the laser removes.

Gear pair creates two matching gears at the right centre distance, as one assembly. In the 3D view they mesh and can turn. Field Meaning Teeth gear 1 / Teeth gear 2 The ratio is teeth 2 ÷ teeth 1. Module, Pressure angle, Backlash, Kerf As for a single gear. Base plate with axle holes Adds a plate with both axle holes at the right distance, with Axle hole diameter and Base plate margin around the tip circles. Bore Per gear. Profile shift gear 1 (Advanced) shifts the small gear; gear 2 gets the opposite shift, so the centre distance stays the same.

A Rack is a straight gear that meshes with a spur gear: rotation becomes linear motion. Field Meaning Number of teeth Length of the rack in teeth (the length is teeth × module × π). Module, Pressure angle Must match the gear. Backlash Split between rack and gear. Backing height Material below the tooth roots. Kerf As for the gear.

Plywood and acrylic from 3 mm work well from module 1.5 up. Smaller modules need a thin, precise beam. Cut a gear pair and test it on two pins before making a larger mechanism; adjust the backlash if it binds. Put a pin through the centre bore instead of relying on the bore of plywood alone: wood wears quickly.

KizamuBeam turns a 3D model (STL, binary or text, or OBJ) into flat parts you can laser. There are two ways, both in Toolbox → 3D slot-together models. When you open or import an STL or OBJ file, or drop it onto the workspace, KizamuBeam asks which one you want. The model is stored once in the project file, so the parts can be edited again later with a double-click.

The model is cut into stacked sheets that you glue back together: heads, figures, reliefs, terrain. Setting Meaning Up in the model Which axis of the file points up. Layers Stacking direction: bottom to top, front to back or left to right. Size (longest side) Size of the finished model in mm. Material thickness Thickness of each sheet. Cross-section Where each sheet takes its outline: the middle of the layer; outside (nothing is missing, sand the steps off); or inside (no layer sticks out). Engrave numbers Each sheet gets its number, counted from the bottom, as a fine engraving on its own "Labels" layer. Smallest area (mm²) Smaller islands are left out, smaller holes filled (Advanced). Kerf Width of the laser cut. Several overlapping bodies in the file are merged per layer. Holes in the mesh up to 0.5 mm are bridged and reported. The check warns about empty layers, layers with several pieces and very many layers. The 3D view shows the stack. Tip: with a wide model, choose the stacking direction (Layers) so the layers are as large as possible: fewer layers, less glueing.

Ribs stand across an axis and slot onto a spine with half slots, like wooden animal kits. Setting Meaning Up in the model Which axis of the file points up. Axis Left–right, front–back or bottom–top: the direction the ribs follow. Spine stands Upright, facing front or sideways. Size (longest side) Size of the finished model. Material thickness Thickness of the board. Rib spacing (center to center) Distance between the ribs. Spine inset Keeps the spine from sticking out between the ribs (0 = full outline). Fit clearance Extra slot width; negative = press fit. Engrave numbers Each rib gets its number; the spine gets the number of the matching rib under each slot. Assembly plan as its own page Adds a page (not lasered) with a view, all part numbers, the assembly order and the parts list. Kerf Width of the laser cut. Where a rib and the spine cross, the shared line is split: the rib is slotted from below, the spine from above, so ribs are pushed onto the spine from above. Rib pieces that reach no spine are left out with a warning.

Animals and figures need more than one spine: a body, legs, a head, a tail. In the drawing area of the dialog (front, side and top view with the model's silhouette) you draw sections, each with its own axis. An axis can be a polyline; ribs then stand across the curve. Each section has a plane position (Center puts it in the middle of the material), its own rib spacing, a radius for the area it owns and an extension of its spine beyond the axis, so a leg plate reaches into the body and slots into the body ribs. The copy button mirrors a section, for example for the second leg. Drag points and lines to change them; in another view, dragging moves the plane. Suggest finds sections automatically as a starting point: the mirror plane of the model becomes the body's spine, legs are traced upward from the floor, and thin ends such as a tail get curved sections of their own. Check and correct the suggestion before creating. More options: Denser at details, down to: where the outline changes quickly (nose, ears), ribs move closer together, down to this spacing. Split plates above (Advanced): spine plates longer than this, for example longer than the bed, are split and joined with a dovetail. Shift spine (Advanced): moves the spine away from the centre. The 3D view shows the assembled model and checks it for collisions; the design check also tests whether the parts can be assembled in some order. Tip: thin parts such as legs need a rib spacing that gives them at least two or three ribs, otherwise they have no hold. Thicker material makes the model sturdier but coarser.

Multi-layer work (Toolbox → 3D slot-together models) turns shapes you designed yourself into a stacked piece: a shadow box, a layered landscape, a relief or a sign with several levels. Unlike the layered model, the layers come from your own drawing, not from a 3D file.

Draw each layer as a closed shape or a group (for example a frame, mountains, trees, the sky). Select them all and choose Multi-layer work in the Toolbox. The dialog lists the selected shapes from bottom to top. Give each plate a Plate name and a Thickness, and move it up or down with Move up one layer / Move down one layer. Create. The shapes stay editable. The 3D view shows them stacked flush, with engravings and the material look of their layer, which makes it easy to judge depth before cutting. To change the order or thicknesses later, select the plates and start Multi-layer work again.

Give each plate its own colour layer if the plates are different materials or colours, so the 3D view shows them correctly. Keep a common outer frame on every plate so the stack lines up when glued. Thin sheets (1 to 3 mm) give a fine relief; use more plates rather than thicker ones.
Both generators are in Toolbox → Mechanics.

A Pulley for toothed belts, with the outside diameter calculated from the pitch and the pitch line offset of the belt. Field Meaning Belt profile GT2 (2, 3 or 5 mm pitch) or HTD (3M, 5M). Number of teeth 8 to 400. Groove clearance Widens every groove so the belt runs in easily (negative values make it tighter). Kerf Width of the laser cut. Bore None, round, D-shaft or with keyway, as for gears. The grooves are round, with the usual groove depth and width for the profile. A belt pulley is usually cut from several layers glued together, with a larger disc on each side as a flange.

A Cam turns rotation into a lifting motion of a follower: for automata, toys and simple mechanisms. One revolution is split into rise, dwell at the top, return and dwell at the bottom. Field Meaning Base circle radius Smallest radius of the cam: the follower is at its lowest here. Lift How far the follower rises. Rise angle Rotation over which the follower rises. Dwell at top Rotation over which it stays at the top. Return angle Rotation over which it falls again. The rest of the turn is the dwell at the bottom. Motion law Cycloidal (low jerk), 5th-degree polynomial or Harmonic. Cycloidal runs smoothest. Follower Roller (with Roller diameter) or Knife edge. Kerf Width of the laser cut. Bore As for gears. The dialog checks the pressure angle and the roller size: if the cam is too steep for the follower, or the roller too large for a hollow in the cam, a warning appears. A larger base circle or a longer rise angle helps.

KizamuBeam works with lasers whose controller runs FluidNC, GRBL, grblHAL, Marlin, Smoothieware or Ruida DSP. That covers most diode lasers and Ruida CO₂ lasers. See Machine compatibility for details.

The easiest way is the setup wizard: Laser → Laser Setup …, or the button in the Laser window. On the very first start of the app it opens by itself. It guides you in five steps from the first connection to a first, safe test job. Connect: pick a device template for your laser or a generic one for your controller, then choose USB or network and connect. KizamuBeam never homes the machine when connecting. Detect: KizamuBeam asks the controller for its firmware and version and reads its settings, such as the work area, the power scale and the laser mode. Check: problems are listed in plain language, for example a different work area, laser mode switched off or homing without limit switches. Settings in KizamuBeam can be applied with one click. Changes on the controller are only suggested, together with the command to undo them, and are sent only after you confirm. Move: the head moves along X and Y with the laser off, and you say where it went. A reversed axis gets a suggested fix. Test job: a small square with a circle at low power, with preview and frame. It starts only after you have confirmed that material and focus, frame, eye protection and exhaust are in order.

Connect the laser with a USB cable, choose USB in the wizard or in the Laser window and pick the port. The baud rate is set in the device settings (115200 for most controllers). Windows: some controllers need a USB driver (often CH340 or CP210x) from the laser’s manufacturer. Linux: your user needs access to serial ports, see Installation.

Controllers with Wi-Fi or Ethernet, such as FluidNC or Ruida DSP, are reached over the network: Telnet on port 23, WebSocket on port 81 (FluidNC; port 80 is tried if 81 does not answer), or UDP on port 50200 (Ruida DSP; keypad port 50207). Enter the address of the controller, for example 192.168.1.50 or fluidnc.local. Search … next to the address field finds FluidNC controllers on your local network. Unstable Wi-Fi With FluidNC, a job can be uploaded to the controller’s SD card or flash and run from there (Laser → FluidNC). With Ruida, Save to controller … stores a named .rd job in the controller’s internal memory. A network dropout then no longer stops the job.

Each laser is stored as a device with its own work area, connection and settings. Switch between them at the top of the Laser window or under Laser → Device → Devices …. Device templates exist for many common lasers (for example Swiitol, Ortur, Atomstack, Sculpfun, xTool, Creality Falcon, Two Trees, Longer, Comgrow, OMTech and Ruida); the workspace always shows the bed of the selected device.

The KizamuBeam Virtual Machine is a separate program that behaves like a FluidNC, GRBL or Ruida controller and shows the job in 3D, burning into virtual material. Download it from the releases page and connect with the device template “KizamuBeam Virtual Machine”.

In this walkthrough you make a small name tag: a rounded rectangle that is cut out and a name that is engraved. It takes about ten minutes and shows the basic workflow you will use for every job. Before you start Your laser should be connected and set up, see Connecting a laser. Without a laser you can follow along anyway and stop before the last step, or try the job on the KizamuBeam Virtual Machine, a virtual laser for testing.

Choose the rectangle tool (Ctrl+R) and drag a rectangle on the workspace. In the numeric edits toolbar at the top, set the width to 80 and the height to 30 (mm). The fields accept formulas, too. Round the corners with the corner radius field in the same bar, for example 4.

Choose the text tool (Ctrl+T), click inside the rectangle and type a name. Pick a font and a height in the text toolbar. Any installed font works, and Google Fonts can be added with File → Fonts …. Press Esc to go back to the select tool. Select the text and the rectangle and centre them on each other with C (horizontal centre) and E (vertical centre).

The colour of an object is its layer, and the layer decides how it is lasered. Select the text and click a colour in the palette at the bottom, for example black. The text now uses that layer. Select the rectangle and click another colour, for example red.

In the layers window on the right: Set the text layer to mode Fill, so that the letters are engraved line by line. Leave the rectangle layer on Line, so that the outline is cut. Enter speed and power for your material. If you do not know them yet, run a material test first (Laser → Tests and Calibration → Material Test) or start from the values your laser’s manufacturer recommends. The material library stores what works. Double-click a layer for more options, such as several passes, line interval, tabs and kerf offset.

Laser → Check Design finds open outlines, double lines and parts that are too small, before you waste material. Press Alt+P for the preview. It plays back the job, shows the travel moves and estimates the time.

Place the material, focus the laser and put on eye protection. In the Laser window choose where the job starts (absolute coordinates, user origin or the current position). Click Frame: the head traces the outline of the job, so you can see whether it fits on the material. Click Start. You can pause and stop at any time and adjust power and speed while the job runs. Stay with your laser Never leave a running laser unattended, keep the lid or a fire extinguisher at hand and make sure the exhaust is running.

File → Save (Ctrl+S) stores the project as a .kzb file, with all images embedded. KizamuBeam also keeps an automatic backup, so open tabs come back after a restart. File → Save as template … turns a project into a reusable template: for a name tag, the name could be a parameter that is asked for every time.

KizamuBeam is free and needs no account or license key. Download the installer for your system from the releases page or the website. System File macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel) KizamuBeam_…_universal.dmg Windows (64-bit) KizamuBeam_…_x64-setup.exe Linux (64-bit) KizamuBeam_…_amd64.AppImage, .deb or .rpm

Open the .dmg file and drag KizamuBeam into the Applications folder. Start KizamuBeam from the Applications folder. The app is not notarized by Apple yet, so on the first start macOS may say that it cannot be checked. Open System Settings → Privacy & Security, scroll down and click Open Anyway. You only need to do this once. If “Open Anyway” does not appear Open the Terminal and run xattr -cr /Applications/KizamuBeam.app Then start KizamuBeam again.

Run KizamuBeam_…_x64-setup.exe. If Windows SmartScreen warns about an unknown publisher, click More info → Run anyway. The installer is not code-signed yet, which is common for young open-source projects. Follow the installer. KizamuBeam then appears in the Start menu.

Pick the package that suits your distribution: AppImage (any distribution): make the file executable and start it. chmod +x KizamuBeam_*_amd64.AppImage ./KizamuBeam_*_amd64.AppImage .deb (Debian, Ubuntu, Linux Mint …): sudo apt install ./KizamuBeam_*_amd64.deb .rpm (Fedora, openSUSE …, stable releases only): sudo dnf install ./KizamuBeam-*.x86_64.rpm USB connection on Linux To talk to a laser over USB, your user usually needs access to serial ports. On most distributions that means membership in the dialout group (on Arch-based systems uucp). Log out and back in after adding yourself: sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER

KizamuBeam checks for new versions and updates itself: Help → Check for Updates …. Under Edit → Settings → General → Updates you choose the update channel: Stable: only finished releases (recommended). Nightly (including pre-releases): a new build every night from the current development state, plus release candidates before each stable version. Try new features earlier and help find bugs. Nightly builds are not tested on real hardware: watch your first job, and files saved with a nightly build may not open in the stable version. If you used the former Beta channel, KizamuBeam switches you to Stable; choose Nightly yourself if you want it.
The user interface: a tour of the main window. Connecting a laser: the setup wizard opens by itself on the very first start.

Area What you find there Menu bar (top) File, Edit, Tools, Arrange, Pages, Laser, View, Window and Help. Main toolbar (below the menu) New, open, save, import and export, undo, clipboard, zoom, 3D view, camera, device settings, design check, preview, grouping, isolation, mirroring and alignment. Numeric edits toolbar Position, size and rotation of the selection. Fields accept formulas with units, such as 100/3 or 2in. With a text selected, the text toolbar appears with font, height and spacing. Tools toolbar (left) Select and edit nodes, draw lines, curves, rectangles, ellipses, polygons and text, button groups for Boolean operations (with the shape builder), contour (offset), path tools and arrays, relations and measuring, and at the end the Toolbox with all generators and special tools. A small ▾ next to a button opens the rest of its group. Project tabs (above the workspace) Several projects open at once, each with its own pages, selection and undo history. Workspace (centre) The laser bed of the selected device. Drag guides out of the rulers. Windows (right) Layers (Cuts), Objects and History; at the bottom right Laser, Move and Console. Palette (bottom) One colour per layer. Click a colour to put the selection on that layer. Status bar (bottom) Pointer position, snapping (“Snap”) and grid (“Grid”). The windows can be moved, docked, grouped as tabs and hidden. Window in the menu bar shows and hides them, and toolbars can be customized.

documents.t: Every object belongs to a layer, and every layer has a colour. The layer decides how the object is lasered: mode (line or fill), speed, power, passes and more. Objects never carry their own laser settings; to laser something differently, put it on another layer. Double-click a layer in the layers window to open its cut settings.

Click selects an object, Shift+click adds to the selection. A marquee to the right selects objects that lie completely inside, a marquee to the left also selects objects it only touches. Click a selected object a second time to switch between scaling and rotating. Arrow keys move the selection by 1 mm (Shift 10 mm, Alt 0.1 mm). Space + drag, the middle mouse button or the mouse wheel move and zoom the view. All shortcuts are listed under Keyboard shortcuts and in the app with F1.
View → Language: English, German, Italian and more. The default follows your system. View → Theme, or the button at the far right of the toolbar: light or dark. The default follows your system.
Edit → Settings … gathers all application preferences in one window with a search field: general, appearance, workspace and snapping, mouse and keyboard, machines and services, extensions and fonts.
Yes. KizamuBeam is licensed GPL-3.0-or-later: no license fee, no subscription, no account, commercial use included.

File → Import (Ctrl+I), drag and drop from the file manager, or paste with Ctrl+V. Format Notes Images: PNG, JPG, BMP, GIF, WebP, TIFF Size from the file’s resolution (254 DPI if none is given). Multi-page TIFF: first page. SVG Paths, basic shapes, transforms, embedded images. Texts are skipped; convert them to paths before saving the SVG. DXF Lines, polylines with arcs, circles, arcs, ellipses, splines and blocks. Units from the file. PDF Paths stay curves, colours map to layers, embedded images and text (as outlines). Every page goes onto its own project page. Adobe Illustrator (.ai) Files from Illustrator 9 onwards (they contain a PDF version); imported like PDF. LightBurn projects (.lbrn2) Shapes, images, groups and layer settings. File → Open makes a new project, Import inserts into the current one. Ruida jobs (.rd) Binary Ruida files (0x88, 0x11, 0x38): vector paths, layer speed, min/max power and air assist. 3D models: STL, OBJ Turned into a layered or rib model of flat parts.

File → Export, also as toolbar buttons. Format Notes SVG Current page, with images DXF Current page, one DXF layer per KizamuBeam layer, curves as exact splines. Images cannot go into DXF. PDF All pages at bed size 1:1, one PDF layer per KizamuBeam layer, images embedded Adobe Illustrator (.ai) Same PDF-compatible file; opens in Illustrator, Inkscape and Affinity G-code (.gcode, .nc) Laser → Save GCode … for the selected device Ruida (.rd) Laser → Save .rd … when a Ruida device is selected PNG Save Processed Bitmap: an image exactly as it would be lasered Texts are exported as outlines.

KizamuBeam talks directly to the controller of your laser and sends G-code or binary Ruida .rd jobs. It works with most diode lasers and CO₂ lasers whose controller runs one of these firmwares: Firmware Connection Notes FluidNC USB, Wi-Fi (Telnet, WebSocket) Configuration editor, jobs from the controller’s SD card or flash, network search GRBL 1.1 USB, Wi-Fi where the controller offers it Real-time status and overrides grblHAL USB, network Like GRBL Marlin USB Sent line by line; position via M114 Smoothieware USB Sent line by line; power from 0 to 1 xTool (USB) USB xTool D1 family; detected by the setup wizard. Status is read only while idle, so the job counts as finished when the last line is accepted. Not yet tested on hardware Ruida DSP Network (UDP 50200/50207), USB serial, .rd file export RDC6442G/S, RDC6445G, RDC6332G, KT332N and compatible CO₂ controllers; binary .rd export/import, direct job streaming, saving named jobs to controller memory, framing and jogging Rotary attachments (roller or chuck, on the Y port or as a separate axis), a motorized Z axis and air assist are supported.

When you create a device, templates for common lasers fill in the work area and settings, for example Swiitol, Ortur, Atomstack, Sculpfun, xTool, Creality Falcon, Two Trees, Longer, Comgrow, OMTech and Ruida. For any other laser, choose the generic template for its controller. The setup wizard then reads the real values from the machine.

Other DSP controllers (such as Trocen/AWC, TopWisdom or Leetro): not supported yet. Galvo lasers: not supported. Lasers with proprietary protocols, such as some xTool models that only talk over the manufacturer’s network protocol.
Reports from real machines help others. Tell us on Discord or in a GitHub issue which laser you use with KizamuBeam and how well it works.

macOS says the app cannot be checked or is damaged. The app is not notarized by Apple yet. Open System Settings → Privacy & Security and click Open Anyway, or run xattr -cr /Applications/KizamuBeam.app in the Terminal. See Installation. Windows SmartScreen blocks the installer. Click More info → Run anyway. The installer is not code-signed yet.

The USB port does not show up. Try another cable: some USB cables only charge and carry no data. Close other programs that might hold the port open (another laser program, a serial terminal). Windows: install the USB driver for your controller (often CH340 or CP210x). Linux: add your user to the dialout group, then log out and back in. The laser is not found over Wi-Fi. Computer and laser must be in the same network. Enter the controller’s IP address instead of a name such as fluidnc.local. With FluidNC, try Search … next to the address field, or switch between Telnet and WebSocket. The machine reports an alarm after connecting. Many controllers start in alarm state until they are homed or unlocked. Home the machine if it has limit switches, otherwise unlock it in the Move window. The Laser window shows the alarm in plain language.

The laser moves but does not fire, or only at full power. The power scale in KizamuBeam (S value for 100 %) must match the controller ($30 on GRBL), and laser mode must be on ($32=1). The setup wizard detects both and offers to fix them. An axis moves the wrong way. Run step 4 (“Move”) of the setup wizard. It detects a reversed axis and suggests the right setting. KizamuBeam says the job does not fit on the bed. Before every job, KizamuBeam checks all moves against the work area. Check the job origin and the start mode in the Laser window (absolute coordinates, user origin or current position), and the work area in the device settings. The job stops when the Wi-Fi drops. With FluidNC, upload the job to the controller and run it from there (Laser → FluidNC).
Ask on Discord or open a GitHub issue. Mention your operating system, KizamuBeam version, laser and firmware.

Each tutorial is a complete project, from the first click to the finished part. They build on Your first project, which shows the basic workflow: draw, assign layers, set speed and power, preview, frame and start. Tutorial You learn Time A box with an engraved lid Box generator, fit calibration, engraving on a panel, 3D view about 45 minutes Name tags from a list Templates, parameters, series from a table about 20 minutes Engraving a photo on wood Image modes, adjusting images, material test for engraving about 30 minutes A layered shadowbox Library motifs, Boolean operations, multi-layer work about 60 minutes The times are for working in KizamuBeam; lasering depends on your machine and material. Want to write a tutorial? Projects you have made with KizamuBeam are a great starting point. See Contributing to the manual, or share your idea on Discord.

In this tutorial you make a closed box of 3 mm plywood, about 100 × 80 × 50 mm, with a name engraved on the lid. The fingers should hold the box together without glue. You need: a sheet of 3 mm plywood (a scrap for the test, a piece of about 300 × 200 mm for the box) and a caliper or ruler.
documents.s: A box with an engraved lid

documents.t: A box only holds when kerf and clearance suit your laser and your material. Measure this once and KizamuBeam remembers it. Measure the plywood with a caliper in several places and note the average, for example 2.9 mm. Choose the material of the cut layer in the layers window, or add it in the material library. Choose Laser → Tests and Calibration → Calibrate Fit …. The test parts appear on a new page. Cut the test parts on a scrap piece with your cutting settings. Measure the square, find the tab and the slot that fit best, and enter the values. KizamuBeam stores kerf and clearance with the material. Details are in Calibrate fit. If you skip this step, start with a kerf of 0.15 mm and a fit clearance of 0 and adjust after the first box.

Open the Toolbox and choose Boxes and Furniture → Finger Joint Box. Set Dimensions to Outside dimensions and enter width 100, depth 80 and height 50. Enter the Material thickness you measured. Set Up to Closed (lid with fingers). With a calibrated material, the dialog already uses its kerf and clearance. Otherwise enter them yourself. Click Create. The six panels appear on the page in a compact layout. They are one parametric part: double-click any panel to change the size later.

Find the lid: it is the panel with the same width and depth as the base. Choose the text tool (Ctrl+T), click on the lid and type a name. Pick a font and a height of about 12 mm. Put the text on its own layer: click another colour in the palette, then set that layer to Fill in the layers window. Select the text and the lid and centre them on each other with C and E. Group the text with the lid (Ctrl+G), so it moves along when the box is rearranged.
documents.s: 3. Engrave the name on the lid

documents.t: Open Window → 3D View. The box is shown assembled, with the name on the lid (tick Engravings). Drag the Explode slider to see how the panels fit together. Red areas mean that two parts collide; check the thickness and clearance if you see any. Laser → Check Design also checks every joint against the calibration and finds open outlines or double lines.

Set speed and power on both layers. Use the values from your material test or the material library. Make sure the engraving layer comes before the cut layer in the layer list, so the panels are engraved before they are cut free. Check the job with the preview (Alt+P), place the plywood, frame and start.

Push the panels together by hand: first the sides onto the base, then the lid. If the fit is too tight, tap the joints with a piece of wood instead of forcing them. For the next box: Too tight: raise the fit clearance by 0.05 mm. Too loose: lower it by 0.05 mm, or use a few drops of wood glue.

Make the lid openable with a lid hinge. Add dividers with the Finger Joint Box with Dividers or a divider insert. Save the project as a template with a parameter for the name: see Name tags from a list.

In this tutorial you make name tags for a group, for example a class or a workshop, from a list of names. You set up the tag once and KizamuBeam lays out one copy per name. You need: the list of names, in a spreadsheet or typed in, and a sheet of material for the tags (3 mm plywood or acrylic works well).

Choose File → New from template … and pick Name tag. The fill-in dialog shows the fields of the template: the name, a Second line, the size and whether the tag gets two holes. Enter a size that suits your material, for example 80 × 30 mm, and confirm. The template is an ordinary project with parameters. Open Window → Parameters to see them: the text on the tag contains {Name}, which is replaced by the value of the parameter. You can also design your own tag: draw it, create a text parameter in the Parameters window and type {Name} in a text.

Choose File → Series from table (CSV) …. Enter the names, one row per tag. You can paste cells copied from a spreadsheet, or load a file with Import CSV …. Under Assign columns, choose which column fills which parameter. Columns whose heading matches a parameter name are assigned automatically. Leave the second line on — keep value — if every tag should show the same text.

Under Layout, choose Grid: as many as fit on the bed, then more pages. Set the spacing between the tags, for example 3 mm. Click Create series. KizamuBeam adds the tags on new pages behind the current one, with the names filled in. Your template page stays as it was, and the table is saved with the project, so you can add names later and create the series again. Long names do not change the size of the tag. Check the pages for names that are too wide for the tag, and shorten them or make the font smaller on the template page before you create the series again.
Select a page with tags, check the layers (engraving on Fill, the outline on Line) and look at the preview (Alt+P). Place the material, frame and start. Then go on with the next page.

Counters and dates: for serial numbers or a date on each job instead of a fixed list, use variable text. Batches of blanks: if you engrave ready-made blanks, cut a jig and use Place on jig slots: variable text counts up per slot. Your own template: File → Save as template … turns your tag into a template that asks for its values, with your own fields and sliders.

In this tutorial you engrave a portrait or a pet photo on a piece of light wood, such as poplar plywood, birch or basswood. Photo engraving is mostly about two things: preparing the image and finding the right speed and power. You need: a photo with good contrast (a face in even light works best), a piece of light, smooth wood, and a scrap of the same wood for the test.

Choose File → Import (Ctrl+I) and pick the photo, or drag it onto the workspace. Scale it to the size you want, for example 100 mm wide. Lock the aspect ratio so the picture is not distorted. Put the image on its own layer by clicking a palette colour.

Remove the background if the subject should stand alone: Tools → Image → Remove Background …. Click the background in the preview, adjust the tolerance and tick Crop to subject. Adjust the image: Tools → Image → Adjust Image …. Wood darkens quickly, so most photos need more brightness and contrast than you would expect. Raise the contrast until the face has clear light and dark areas, and sharpen a little. Use the comparison with the original and the 1:1 view. To give the photo a shape, draw an ellipse or a rounded rectangle over it, select both and choose Tools → Image → Apply mask to image.

Double-click the image to open the layer settings with the Image section, and choose the Image Mode: Atkinson or Floyd-Steinberg are the safe choice for photos on wood. Atkinson keeps more contrast, which suits wood well. Grayscale varies the power instead of setting dots. It only works well on materials that darken evenly, and needs a careful test. Newsprint gives a round-dot look that suits large pictures seen from further away. The workspace shows the result at laser resolution; zoom in to judge it. Set the line interval to suit your laser's spot, typically 0.08 to 0.1 mm for a diode laser (about 250 to 300 lines per inch). A finer interval than the spot only makes the picture darker and muddier. Set an Overscan so the edges of the picture are not darker.

Choose Laser → Tests and Calibration → Material Test …. Set up a grid for engraving, for example speed in the rows and power in the columns, with the same line interval as the photo. Run the test on the scrap of the same wood. Pick the cell that is dark but not burned. Evaluate Material Test … can do this from a photo of the test. Apply the values to the image layer, or save them in the material library for next time. More in Materials and tests.
documents.s: 4. Find the settings with a material test

documents.t: Look at the preview (Alt+P) and check the time: a photo takes much longer than text. Focus carefully: a blurred spot makes a blurred picture. The focus test helps. Place the wood, frame and start. Keep the exhaust running, because engraving wood makes a lot of smoke.

Problem Try Too dark, details are lost More brightness in Adjust Image, a larger line interval, or less power. Too pale, little contrast More contrast, or more power or less speed. Lines or stripes Check that the belts are tight and the line interval is not finer than the spot. Overscan avoids darker edges. Brown haze around the picture Mask the wood with tape before engraving, or wipe it with a damp cloth afterwards. For dark materials that turn light when lasered, such as anodised aluminium or painted slate, tick Negative Image.

documents.t: A shadowbox is a picture made of several stacked layers, each with a cut-out, so the scene gets depth. In this tutorial you build a small landscape with five layers: a back panel, sky with a moon, mountains, trees and a front frame. You need: five pieces of 3 mm plywood or thick card, about 150 × 150 mm each, and wood glue. Coloured card or painted layers look especially good.
Every layer has the same outer frame, so the stack stays flush. From back to front: Layer Content 1 Back panel, closed 2 Sky: a frame with a round moon cut out 3 Mountains 4 Trees 5 Front frame

Draw a square of 150 × 150 mm (rectangle tool, Ctrl+R, then enter the size in the numeric toolbar). Draw a second square of 130 × 130 mm and centre it on the first (C and E). Copy the outer square first (Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V) and move the copy aside: it becomes the back panel. Select both squares of the frame and choose Boolean Difference (Tools → Boolean Operations). You now have a frame.

Copy the frame for the layers 2 to 5 (Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V) and place the copies side by side. Sky: draw a square that fills the opening and overlaps the frame, and a circle for the moon on it. Subtract the circle with Boolean Difference, then Weld the result to the frame. Mountains: draw a mountain line with the Lines and curves tool (Ctrl+L) across the opening, closing it along the bottom of the frame, and Weld it to the frame. Trees: open Window → Library, search for "tree" and drag a few trees onto the workspace. Let them stand on a hill drawn along the bottom and Weld everything to the frame. Front frame: the frame alone, or with a few branches from the library hanging into the opening. Keep every layer as one closed outline: check that parts that should hold together really touch the frame. Loose islands would fall out.

Select all five layers. Choose Toolbox → 3D Slot-Together Models → Multi-layer work. Order the layers from bottom to top: back panel first, front frame last. Give each a name and a thickness of 3 mm. Click Create. Open Window → 3D View. The layers are stacked flush, and you can turn the view to judge the depth. If a layer covers too much of the one behind it, change the shapes and look again. To change the order or thickness later, select the layers and start Multi-layer work again. More in Multi-layer work.

Put all outlines on a cut layer and run Laser → Check Design: it finds open outlines and parts that are too small. Cut the layers. Small details such as tree branches need a slower speed or an extra pass to cut through cleanly. Paint or colour the layers if you like, before gluing. Glue the stack from back to front, pressing the outer frames together so they stay flush. Clamp or weight it while the glue dries.

An LED strip between the back panel and the sky layer makes a night light. Engrave stars on the back panel with a fill layer before cutting. For a relief from a 3D model instead of your own drawing, use the layered model.
